This paper reports on the observation of two types of fluctuations, angle and intensity, in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC's 5.02 TeV collision energy. Angle fluctuations refer to variations in the direction of particle emission relative to the reaction plane, a phenomenon that has been well-documented in small and medium-sized systems. Intensity fluctuations, on the other hand, pertain to variations in final particle numbers when comparing different sub-systems of the reaction. Our findings indicate that angle fluctuations remain consistent with expectations based on initial conditions, whereas intensity fluctuations exhibit a higher magnitude than predicted by models of initial condition fluctuations. These findings hold across a range of transverse momentum thresholds, from 0.1 to 1 GeV, and are consistent with theoretical interpretations that attribute their origin to early stages of heavy-ion collisions. Notably, our results also reveal a linear relationship between angle and intensity fluctuations, which may be influenced by initial condition properties, final-state hadronization, or other factors. This discovery highlights the significance of further investigation into the underlying causes of these fluctuations and their potential utility as probes of heavy-ion collisions. Our analysis employed data from the ALICE detector for collisions with a centrality range of 0-80%. Our findings are also relevant to similar measurements in other heavy-ion experiments and may be compared to theoretical predictions from fluid dynamical models of heavy-ion collisions. Our results are further supported by similar findings for proton-proton collisions at 7.0 TeV, which indicate that the origin of these fluctuations may be inherent to strong interaction dynamics rather than being influenced by initial condition properties. Our analysis also explored the potential utility of these fluctuations as sources of intrinsic elliptical flow by examining the ratio of angle to intensity fluctuations as a function of centrality and transverse momentum threshold. Our results suggest that the proportion of intrinsic elliptical flow may be as high as 20% in the most central collisions. Our findings are available in the form of tables and figures in the supplementary materials. The process of integrating data from multiple sources into a unified table structure is a complex task. This integration is further complicated by the presence of inconsistencies, where some data may disagree due to differing source representations or because some data is missing. In such cases, additional information in the form of conditional equalities, known as functional dependencies, may be utilized to enhance the integration. However, the existence of inconsistencies raises issues with the validity of conditional equalities. This paper proposes a method for refining conditional equalities to account for existing inconsistencies and presents a sound and complete axiomatization of this refined form. This axiomatization enables us to determine if a set of refined conditional equalities is consistent with a given table, even if it contains missing values. This consistency check can be performed in polynomial time. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to modify a set of original conditional equalities into a equivalent and consistent set of refined conditional equalities in a time that is polynomial relative to the size of the result. This process involves an initial examination of the table and its associated conditional equalities, followed by a series of iterations that progressively refine the conditional equalities based on observations made during an incremental discovery process. This process is efficient because it is guided by a concept of "characteristic pairs" that encapsulates the key information from the table and its associated conditional equalities, and can be updated locally as new data becomes available. Creating robots that can efficiently manipulate objects in complex environments is a significant challenge, largely due to the need for a robust understanding of object shapes and their three-dimensional structures. To address this, a key requirement is the development of object representations that are invariant to rotations in three-dimensional space. In this work, we present a novel approach to constructing neural networks that generate descriptors for objects in a manner independent of their orientation, using only a single 2D image as input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by utilizing the generated descriptors in a data-driven learning framework for grasping and manipulating objects in three-dimensional space from multiple viewpoints. The resulting representations and learning framework were found to improve the success rates of grasping and manipulation tasks from multiple angles, with the former increasing by 12% and the latter by 15% respectively. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/PRPR-UoE/NeuralDescriptorFields.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from monocular images is a highly challenging task due to the limited nature of visual information. This challenge is compounded by the need to estimate a scene's full 3D structure, which requires both a 3D point cloud and a normal map to accurately define surfaces. To address this, we propose an end-to-end framework called DeepHMap++, which simultaneously generates a normal map and estimates a scene's full 3D DoF pose through a two-stage process. Initially, we pretrain our network to produce a normal map by leveraging a feature extractor and a set of U-shape encoders. In the second stage, we incorporate the generated normal map into the input and estimate the 3D pose using a combination of correspondence and grouping cues. Our results show that DeepHMap++ achieves superior performance on the COX dataset, surpassing the current state of the art by a significant margin of 7.3 points in the MAP metric. To further demonstrate its efficacy, we apply DeepHMap++ to the SAPIEN dataset, obtaining a 10.6% relative improvement in the 3D IoU metric compared to the current top-performing method. To reduce training costs, we have also explored a set of efficient training strategies for DeepHMap++. However, despite its utility, determining an optimal length for time steps in LMD can be challenging, as it depends on multiple factors including friction coefficients, bond lengths, and potential energy surface characteristics. In an attempt to address this issue, a systematic investigation of time step lengths was conducted for LMD in conjunction with the MMVB method of intramolecular potential energy calculations. As a result, a set of time step length recommendations was established for various molecular types, including those with single, double, and non-bonded interactions. This study investigates the seal formation in front of a moving sphere in a liquid, a phenomenon relevant to various contexts including gear lubrication. High-speed video recordings of a sphere entering a liquid are analyzed to better understand the relationship between the sphere's speed, the distance it takes to form a seal, and the resulting seal shape. For slower speeds, the sphere creates a seal quickly, with the time required decreasing in proportion to the square of its increased speed. However, at higher speeds, this relationship changes, and the time it takes to form a seal no longer depends on the viscosity of the liquid, instead being influenced by the pressure it generates and the distance it takes to form a seal. The pressure it produces also deviates from expected behavior at these higher speeds. The time it takes to form a seal and the resulting seal shape are influenced by the angle of the leading edge of the seal, which varies with the sphere's speed. The minimum distance it takes to form a seal decreases in proportion to the square of its increased speed in the middle speed regime but remains constant in the higher speed regime. The shape of the seal changes with the sphere's speed, influenced by its Reynolds number. The formation of a seal in the higher speed regime is also compared to the flow around a stationary sphere with a free surface, with notable differences in the shape of the seal and the flow around it. The time it takes to form a seal and the resulting seal shape are predicted using numerical flow simulations, which generally match the observed patterns but also reveal additional features of the flow and the seal shape not captured by the video recordings. The numerical flow simulations also provide a more detailed understanding of the flow around the sphere and the seal formation process, which may be applicable to other contexts beyond the specific conditions of this study. Our study of the magnetic and electronic properties of cupricite CuFe2S3, using X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction, reveals that the local magnetic moments of iron and copper ions differ, with approximately 2.5 μB per iron site and 0.3 μB per copper site. This distinction is supported by theoretical modeling of the atomic and magnetic structures. The distinct magnetic and electronic behaviors of iron and copper are key factors in understanding the unusual electrical conductivity patterns observed in this compound. The unique combination of orbital filling in the iron and copper ions, along with the unusual arrangement of atoms and the magnetic interactions between them, contribute to the complex electronic and magnetic properties of cupricite. This information is also relevant for understanding similar properties in other compounds, such as the A-site and B-site orbital filling in perovskites. This study highlights the value of X-ray absorption spectroscopy in studying the local properties of materials, and the importance of considering the orbital filling of electrons in transition metals in perovskite compounds. A promising area of research involves the study of excitons in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides, particularly for their potential in quantum computing. Recently discovered mechanisms such as interlayer excitons and trions offer improved longevity and robustness of excitons. In this study, we theoretically investigate an unusual phenomenon in bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides - an extremely large and long-lived Rabi oscillation without the need for an external magnetic field. This unusual behavior is made possible by utilizing the strong spin-orbit interaction and long-range Coulomb interaction between electrons in these materials. This result provides an unprecedented means of controlling excitons without a magnetic field and offers a large Rabi oscillation period of ~20 ps and a long-lived component of ~10 ps, making this material an ideal candidate for robust and durable quantum operations. This outcome is further confirmed through the direct observation of huge Rabi oscillations in MoSe2 and WSe2 layers. This discovery paves the way for exploring quantum operations in this material and offers a means of achieving robust and durable quantum operations in a previously unachievable time frame. This finding also highlights the significance of spin-orbit interaction in these materials and provides an explanation for the absence of huge Rabi oscillations in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides. We introduce a technique for creating parametric polymer models using linear regression, and then use these models in an integer optimization framework to predict molecular structures that minimize a specified energy metric. Our approach differs from traditional force field modeling methods by utilizing linear regression to derive parameters, which allows us to consider complex reactions and transformations as polynomial combinations of elemental properties. This technique enables us to generate new polymers by applying optimization to the integer lattice representation of molecules, and our results include predicted energy minimization solutions for polyethylene and polyvinyl chloride chains. Our method can be applied to create new polymers by optimizing reaction pathways, and we demonstrate this capability by generating an energy-minimized polyamide-6 structure using an integer optimization algorithm. Our results highlight the potential for using machine learning in conjunction with integer optimization to create new materials, and we discuss the limitations and potential improvements to our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangyangf/ChemML. Our results for polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, and polyamide-6 are included in the supplementary materials. A novel approach for automatically identifying and outlining neoplasms in the esophagus using CT scans has been developed. This method employs a unique Dense Attention Unet structure that combines the benefits of attention and dense features, and utilizes a two-stage approach to segment the images. In the training phase, the model uses an attention-based mechanism to assign varying levels of importance to different image features, and then employs a combination of the original and encoded features in the subsequent stage. In the prediction phase, a separate set of features is generated for each CT scan, and these features are then used to define a boundary for outlining the neoplasm. This method has been tested on a dataset of 100 CT scans, and the results show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, while also being computationally efficient. Code for this work is publicly available on GitHub. Multilingual individuals can typically understand languages beyond their native tongue to some extent, and many often switch between languages when communicating, a phenomenon known as code-switching. In contrast, code-mixing involves blending two languages into a third, hybrid one. While prevalent in online platforms and social media, code-mixing poses a significant challenge for NLP applications. This issue is particularly acute due to the absence of a standardized code to represent mixed languages and the limited availability of large datasets. In this paper, we examine the code-mixing challenge in NLP through the lens of four critical tasks: sentiment analysis, language identification, machine translation, and text classification. In each section, we explore both existing research and potential factors contributing to the prevalence of code-mixing, including cultural, historical, and technological influences. Furthermore, we discuss potential avenues for future research, including the impact of code-mixing on pre-trained multilingual models and the role of graph-based methods in language analysis. By exploring these aspects, we aim to shed light on the complexities of code-mixing and its implications for NLP research. This work is an invitation to the NLP community to engage with the challenges posed by code-mixing and to explore new research directions in this area. This work is an extension of our previous workshop paper presented at the 2022 EMNLP CodeMix track. With this paper, we provide a more comprehensive overview of the code-mixing challenge, including additional sections on the challenges posed by code-mixing for machine translation and text classification, as well as new sections on the historical and cultural context of code-mixing. We also include a new section on the potential applications of graph-based methods to code-mixing. We hope this expanded version will be beneficial to the NLP community. The primary objective of image description generation can be viewed as an attempt to create a system of image representation that is analogous to written language. This ideal representation would enable various applications that rely on the analysis of natural language, such as visual-based question answering and image retrieval. To evaluate the effectiveness of image description generation, a relevant metric is essential. Although the use of human reference descriptions as standards for assessment has been widely adopted, there are concerns regarding its limitations. This paper examines the potential benefits and drawbacks of incorporating diverse human descriptions for assessment and discusses a statistical approach to select the most suitable descriptions for evaluation. Experimental results on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that a carefully curated set of descriptions yields a more accurate representation of the underlying distribution of human descriptions, thereby providing a more reliable assessment of image description generation. This is particularly evident when the diversity of descriptions is high, as it reduces the overestimation of the automatic evaluation metric. This paper also presents a method for estimating the distribution of human descriptions and demonstrates the utility of this estimation in exploring the underlying distribution of descriptions and identifying instances of description generation bias. This is shown to occur in the COCO dataset, particularly with regard to the attribute of object size. A comprehensive study of Ta$_2$O$_5$ using ab-initio simulations reveals multiple possible crystal structures for this complex oxide, which can exist in both amorphous and crystalline forms.  By comparing simulated structures to experimental data, discrepancies in lattice parameters are addressed, while differences in local and long-range ordering are explored through Monte Carlo simulations.  Results indicate that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a disordered, non-periodic $\gamma$-alumina-like structure, with simulations demonstrating that this structure is stable across various temperatures and pressures.  Notably, previous reports of a monoclinic Ta$_2$O$_5$ phase are disputed, with simulations instead indicating a pseudomonoclinic phase that arises from disorder rather than low-symmetry crystallography.  Further research is suggested to investigate the effects of defects and impurities on Ta$_2$O$_5$'s local and long-range ordering.  This study highlights the utility of combining ab-initio simulations with Monte Carlo methods to elucidate the complex structure of this challenging material.  The resulting understanding of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s crystal structure is expected to inform the development of functional materials and device applications.  The approach employed in this study can also be applied to other complex, disordered materials. An analytical framework known as the Big Geographic Sort (BGS) categorizes US cities into three groups based on economic factors: those that are highly affluent, moderately affluent, and economically struggling. Research suggests that this classification affects how people process and share information on social media platforms. This study examines the influence of the BGS on the spread of misinformation on Reddit among a large sample of users. Controlling for individual factors and using a novel method to identify and label misinformation posts, the analysis reveals that users from economically struggling cities are more susceptible to sharing misinformation than those from more affluent areas. This increased susceptibility is more pronounced when the misinformation aligns with users' economic interests or positions. Furthermore, the study finds that users from struggling cities rely more heavily on social connections to validate information, whereas users from more affluent areas rely more on institutional sources of authority. The findings suggest that the BGS may contribute to the persistence of misinformation by creating an information ecosystem in struggling cities characterized by economic identity-based narratives, social validation, and a distrust of institutions. This research highlights the limitations of generalizing findings from online data to offline contexts and the importance of considering the specific economic and social conditions of local communities in struggling cities. The study also offers implications for understanding the sources of misinformation and the challenges of combating its spread in these communities. The findings can be applied to other domains of information diffusion, beyond the study of misinformation. Humans naturally generate rich audio during interactions with robots, consisting of speech, gestures, and physical manipulation sounds. To enhance robot teaching effectiveness, it's crucial for robots to effectively comprehend the underlying patterns of audio in instruction. To address this challenge, we conducted an experiment in which human instructors taught various manipulation tasks to robots using the PR2 arm. The audio from these teaching sessions was analyzed to extract features, and several machine learning approaches were evaluated to predict three key aspects of the task: intended action, object selection, and completion status. Our findings reveal that, although certain features related to the duration of speech are predictive, the majority of predictive value lies in the non-acoustic aspects of the audio. Furthermore, by integrating additional contextual information, our models achieved a significant improvement in predicting the intended action, with an increase from 0.45 to 0.85 in the F1 score. Our research highlights the importance of considering the contextual background when predicting the content of human instructions. Our dataset, comprising over 13 hours of audio from teaching sessions, along with corresponding labels and feature representations, is available for public use and can serve as a foundation for developing more advanced models to enhance the effectiveness of human-robot teaching. In the future, we plan to explore the integration of visual data and speech recognition outputs to further enhance the performance of our models. Our study demonstrates that effective prediction of human teaching intentions is achievable but highlights the limitations of acoustic data alone. Our findings can be applied to various human-robot interaction scenarios, not limited to teaching. Our dataset is available at https://yukezeng.github.io/human-robot-interaction-audio/}.

Conversational interfaces are becoming increasingly prevalent in our daily lives and it is essential to ensure the reliability of these systems that are now widely used. Although manual testing methods are feasible for small-scale projects, they become impractical for big undertakings like customer support chatbots with millions of users. To address the growing need for automated testing in this area, we present a testing framework that enables developers to create automated tests for a wide range of conversational systems. Our system allows developers to write tests in a user-friendly natural language style and features a robust set of automated testing tools to evaluate the correctness of their bots. We have successfully applied our testing framework to test a real-world production chatbot used by millions of users. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights for future development. Our testing framework is available at https://github.com/ConversationalAI/QuickTalk. Or you can access it via our website at https://www.conversationailab.com/quicktalk.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly effective approach to address the data sparsity challenge in recommendation systems. Most existing methods focus on intra-domain optimization and use intra- and inter-domain similarity to perform interpolation and extrapolation. However, they often overlook the attribute preference of users. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework called MSDCR, which leverages enhanced comprehensive attribute preference learning to guide inter-domain extrapolation. Specifically, MSDCR employs an attention-based mechanism to dynamically weigh the importance of attributes and learns a comprehensive preference for each user by aggregating attribute preferences across all domains. We evaluate MSDCR on three real-world datasets and compare its performance with six state-of-the-art baselines using two evaluation metrics. Convex optimization over natural conic expressions, a broad class of expressions defined by various conic forms, is a versatile tool that has been successfully applied to a wide range of problems across fields such as energy, transportation, and finance. Despite its utility, this method has seen limited use due to the requirement that expressions be formulated using specific conic representations, which can be challenging, especially for complex data structures and nonlinear functions. This issue is compounded by the need for a suitable conic representation for each new problem, with no standard approach established across different disciplines. This website aims to address this constraint by providing a collection of pre-defined conic representations for common functions and structures, along with tools for automatically generating custom representations. This approach simplifies the use of conic optimization for an array of applications, including nonconvex problems, semidefinite programming, and robust optimization. This website also serves as an incubator for user-generated submissions of new functions and structures, with the goal of establishing a unified standard for conic representations across different domains. This way, researchers and practitioners can share and utilize existing representations, and contribute to an ever-growing repository of pre-defined conic representations. This will be achieved through an open-source Julia package called Hypatia, with a simple and intuitive syntax for defining and manipulating conic expressions and their corresponding representations. This package can be easily integrated into existing optimization solvers, including JuMP, MOSEK, and SDO.jl. This website provides documentation, examples, and a gallery of pre-defined conic representations for common functions and structures, as well as user-generated submissions. This approach has been successfully applied to a range of problems, including a non-convex portfolio optimization problem, a semidefinite programming relaxation of the quadratic knapsack problem, and a robust optimization problem for demand response in smart grids. This website is available at https://hypatia.julia.gitlab.io/. This approach has been presented at the 2022 INFORMS Annual Meeting. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a crucial diagnostic tool, and its applications in the brain are particularly diverse.  However, the image quality can be significantly impacted by various factors, including the use of multiple sequences, differing field strengths, and the presence of pathology.  These variations necessitate comprehensive quality assurance (QA) procedures to ensure that the acquired images meet the required standards for different clinical and research purposes.  Artificial intelligence (AI) holds the promise to enhance MRI protocols and streamline the QA process through automated image assessment.  This paper presents a novel approach to training an automatic image assessment system for multi-sequence, multi-field-strength, and multi-pathology MRI brain scans.  The proposed method leverages a combination of data augmentation and knowledge-based techniques to ensure that the system can generalize effectively across different brain MRI scans.  The results are demonstrated using publicly available MRI datasets, and the potential applications of this work in the context of MRI protocol optimization and QA procedures are discussed. In cooperative tasks involving multiple agents, a common issue arises when some agents excel at one phase of the task while others excel at another phase. This challenge is particularly evident in meetings like the one described in this study, where two agents work together to achieve two separate goals within a set time limit. A key problem in this context is ensuring that the agents' individual motivations align with the overall progress towards the shared objectives. Our approach addresses this issue by introducing an incentive mechanism based on a driving metaphor. In this framework, each agent's progress towards their individual goals is compared to a target speed, and the resulting differences are used to guide their actions. We tested this model in a meeting scenario with two agents working towards two separate goals within a set time limit. The results show that the model leads to a significant increase in the chances of achieving both goals compared to a baseline model. Additionally, the model adapts to new situations more effectively than a standard recurrent meeting model. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangliu/MRMDBI.

We analyzed the variation in luminosity distance of 115 Type Ia Supernovae from the Pantheon sample, specifically looking at their intrinsic brightness, to see how it changes with position on the sky. This change, caused by gravitational lensing, is a key prediction of Einstein's theory of gravity and has been mathematically described as a random fluctuation. By averaging this distribution, we calculated an expected shift of about 0.68 magnitudes, which we compared to the actual change observed in the data. This actual change was found to be 0.83 magnitudes when considering the full sample, but varied when broken down by color, with a more significant change of 0.96 magnitudes observed in the bluer supernovae. When accounting for the expected shift, we found a lensing-induced brightening of about 0.15 magnitudes in the red supernovae, with the bluer supernovae showing a more significant change of 0.18 magnitudes. An intriguing aspect of ideal organ allocation models is the way they handle incompatible kidney transplants. In many real-world scenarios, patients have multiple incompatible transplants, and these transplants can be both clinically and socially complex. For example, a patient may have multiple incompatible transplants from different family members, making it difficult to determine priorities in allocation decisions. Another example involves a donor who wishes to donate a kidney to multiple recipients but is limited by compatibility restrictions. To address these challenges, we propose an ideal allocation model based on the concept of "worth" that assigns a numerical value to the value of each transplant for each patient. This model allows for the comparison of multiple incompatible transplants across different patients. We also explore ways to determine the optimal allocation of kidneys to patients by maximizing overall value, and discuss computational methods for achieving this goal. Our results show that this model can be efficiently solved using standard algorithms, and that it provides fair and efficient allocation of kidneys even in the presence of multiple incompatible transplants. Our research also highlights the importance of taking into account the social aspects of organ donation and transplantation. Our model can be applied to other organ transplantation scenarios, and provides a framework for addressing other complex allocation problems. Our findings are supported by numerical examples and graphical illustrations. Recent studies comparing the effectiveness of various word representations have relied on tasks that assess their ability to capture semantic relationships, despite the lack of a universally accepted benchmark. Another area of interest involves evaluating the ability of these representations to convey the emotional nuances of words, specifically the polarity labels proposed by Loughran and McDonald. We examine multiple pre-trained models on three tasks that have been previously used to evaluate the quality of word representations, and find that they excel at capturing complex semantic relationships but struggle with local representations. Furthermore, we find that current representations are adept at predicting the emotional polarity of words but may overfit to the training data. We also explore the limitations of the existing benchmarks and discuss potential avenues for improvement. We conclude that the current standards for evaluating word representations are insufficient and that a more comprehensive framework is necessary to accurately reflect their performance. To address this limitation, we present the MultiTalk Dataset, a significant expansion of the previous TalkDB, featuring over 300 unique dialogue scenarios with multiple branches, loops, and divergent paths. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the value of the MultiTalk Dataset in uncovering the underlying decision-making processes behind different dialogue systems and highlight the importance of evaluating the diversity of responses generated by these systems. However, when considering SLE on a surface with multiple ends, a single Gaussian free field is not sufficient to describe the behavior of all the curves. In this study, we show that for a certain type of surface topologies, there exists a single Gaussian free field that can capture the combined behavior of all the curves, effectively treating their interaction as if they were a single curve driven by the field. This is achieved by reformulating the driving forces of the SLE as discrete log-gases and applying an approximation method that treats the interaction between the curves as weak, allowing us to use a Gaussian free field to describe the combined behavior. This is an advancement over previous work that only considered the interaction between two curves, and it provides a new universal conformal field theory that can be applied to more complex surfaces. This is particularly relevant to the study of random planar lattices and can be used to model the behavior of systems like the O(n) loop model and the Q-state Potts model. This is a significant finding as it shows that the asymptotic behavior of the Potts model at criticality is a universal, rather than a model-dependent, property. A key aspect of general relativity is the fundamental equivalence principle, which postulates that all physical laws must exhibit the same invariance under coordinate transformations. This invariance is the basis for the geometric representation of gravity. To extend this concept to nonlocal gravity, we must modify the geometric representation. In this nonlocal version, gravity is represented as a scalar field with a specific mathematical property, rather than a tensor field. To achieve this, we use a mathematical tool called a "memory matrix" that connects the nonlocal property to the geometric representation. To maintain the equivalence principle, we must ensure that the memory matrix is independent of coordinate transformations. In this paper, we outline the steps to achieve this independent memory matrix, which results in a nonlocal gravity model. We also compare our approach to alternative nonlocal gravity models proposed by M\"oller and Mavrot. Furthermore, we derive the nonlocal Einstein field equations using both a variational approach and a semi-variational approach. We demonstrate that the nonlocal Einstein equations can be represented in a form that is analogous to the original Einstein equations, albeit with a distinct nonlocal correction term. We also explore the implications of these nonlocal corrections on the behavior of gravitational waves. In particular, we examine the effect of these corrections on the frequency spectrum of gravitational waves emitted by a binary neutron star merger event. We find that the nonlocal gravity model causes a shift in the frequency spectrum, albeit a minimal one. We also propose a modified version of the nonlocal gravity model, which we term "dynamical nonlocal gravity," such that the memory matrix is dependent on the covariant derivative of the metric tensor. We derive the corresponding nonlocal Einstein equations for this modified version. We find that this modified nonlocal gravity model results in a nonlocal correction term that is analogous to the cosmological constant in the original Einstein equations. We also examine the implications of this nonlocal correction term on the behavior of gravitational waves. We find that this nonlocal correction term causes a shift in the frequency spectrum of gravitational waves emitted by a binary neutron star merger event. We propose that this modified nonlocal gravity model could potentially explain the observed shift in the frequency spectrum of gravitational waves emitted by some binary neutron star merger events. We also propose that this modified nonlocal gravity model could potentially explain the observed large-scale structure of the universe. We propose that this modified nonlocal gravity model could potentially be tested using future high-precision measurements of the frequency spectrum of gravitational waves emitted by binary neutron star merger events.

Given a graph representing romantic connections between n males and n females, where each individual is part of a clique of size k, we seek to determine the minimum number of additional connections required among the females, so that no child is born with a genetic disorder caused by one of the six known autosomal recessive diseases listed in the CEPH (Centre d'Etude du Polymorphisme Humain) dataset. This problem can be formulated as a bilevel integer programming problem with a fixed upper bound of (n choose 2) * 6^2 on the number of possible instances, enabling the application of a brute-force algorithm with a running time of O(1.83^n) and a corresponding FPT solution using a parameter-independent additional space of O(n). This FPT solution can be further improved to a nested dynamic programming approach using additional space of O(k^3+ n), allowing the solution of instances beyond the originally defined enumerable set. This nested dynamic programming approach is particularly efficient for instances with a large but fixed number of females. To mitigate heat-related issues and electrical power consumption in high-performance computing, a common practice is to operate CPU frequencies well below their maximum potential. However, determining the optimal frequency for a given workload is a complex task that varies greatly depending on the application. To address this challenge, we developed a statistical approach to estimate the distribution of execution time for a wide range of tasks. Based on this model, we identified a "sweet spot" frequency that minimizes average execution time by 15% compared to traditional approaches, while also offering a 10% reduction in average power consumption. Our findings demonstrate that for real-world workloads, it's possible to reduce CPU frequency from 4 GHz to 1.5 GHz while maintaining acceptable performance degradation. Our research includes a dataset of efficient frequency configurations for various benchmarks and real-world workloads, including those from the CloudSuite, Memcached, and YARC benchmarks, as well as production databases and web applications. Our results highlight the potential for a 2.5x increase in CPU density without significant performance loss, and a 1.5x decrease in power consumption without noticeable slowdowns. Our research is applicable to various fields, including high-performance computing, cloud infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, and provides a foundation for further exploration into efficient frequency optimization. Our research is ongoing under the name HyperDegrade, and we invite the community to collaborate and expand our findings. Our code and dataset are available online.

High dimensional kernel functions in supervised learning methods can lead to significant computational issues due to the extensive cost of quadratic operations. This challenge can be addressed by using kernel estimation techniques based on random Fourier features. However, such methods rely on kernel data being independent of its features, which isn't universally applicable. This paper presents a novel approach to estimating high-dimensional kernel functions using random Fourier features while accounting for data dependencies. We derive an efficient method for estimating the sum of kernel functions, and demonstrate that this approach preserves the bias and variance properties of the original kernel function. Furthermore, we show that this estimation is accurate enough to substitute linear transformations of the original kernel function in a neural network. Experimental results across various classification and regression tasks show that our approach provides comparable performance to independent kernel estimation. This improvement is particularly evident when using feature extractors, and our method can be easily applied to both parametric and non-parametric kernel functions. The avalanche dynamics is a mathematical model that describes how a system responds to disturbances or shocks. Based on this framework, we investigate the spread of a message through a network using a Cayley tree structure. By analyzing the distribution of information dissemination among nodes, we find that the standard avalanche approach leads to an incorrect conclusion about the spread of information, revealing an error in a previous study's result. By directly analyzing the probability distribution of node states, we derive an expression for the distribution of the state of any given node, which is shown to follow a specific non-trivial form that differs from the findings of the previous study. Furthermore, we identify an important condition required to maintain the stability of the system. Additionally, we examine two specific scenarios: a uniform distribution of node states and a distribution characterized by a finite average path length, and provide explicit expressions for the distribution of node states in these cases. Notably, the standard avalanche assumption yields an exponential distribution of node states in these two scenarios. The error in the previous study's result is highlighted by comparing our findings with the existing literature. The analysis presented in this study can be applied to other network structures by identifying the key condition required to extend the standard avalanche assumption to more complex networks. The relevance of the average degree of the network to its stability is also demonstrated. The distribution of node states in the beta-leaf network provides an example of how to generalize the results of this study to other networks. The standard avalanche assumption can lead to incorrect conclusions about the behavior of complex systems, as seen in the example of a beta-leaf network with a non-integer average degree. The possibility of the standard avalanche assumption producing a power-law distribution of node states in certain networks is also explored. The analysis presented in this study can be applied to other areas of study, such as percolation theory, by examining the distribution of the number of open edges in a random bond network on a Cayley tree structure. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the Casimir effect and quantum fluctuations in optical cavities. To overcome this limitation, a new design called the sloshing-Sagnitc interferometer is proposed by modifying the optical cavity in a Michelson interferometer. This design involves dividing the mirror that forms one end mirror of the Michelson interferometer into two separate mirrors, with a gap of a few micrometers in between. This results in a reduction of the optical cavity length, thereby increasing the high-frequency sensitivity of the gravitational wave detector. In addition to this design change, it is also suggested to use a recycling mirror in the sloshing-Sagnitc interferometer to enhance its sensitivity further. This can be achieved by placing the recycling mirror close to one of the small mirrors, which would also reduce the optical cavity length to its minimum possible value. This design has the potential to increase the sensitivity of the gravitational wave detector to specific frequencies, potentially allowing it to detect gravitational waves with frequencies of up to 10 times higher than current detectors. This improvement in sensitivity can be realized with the production of more precise small mirrors, which are now available with surface accuracy of 20 nanometers. This design has also been applied to other types of gravitational wave detectors, including optical lattice and photonic crystal-based sensors. This design can be further optimized by adjusting the angle of the small mirrors to enhance the sensitivity of the detector. This design has also been compared to other types of gravitational wave detectors, including LIGO+, TIGA, and TIGA+, to identify its unique features and areas of improvement. This design can also be realized using a combination of micro-electromechanical systems and nano-imprint lithography. This design has the potential to increase the sensitivity of the gravitational wave detector to a wide range of frequencies, from 10 to 1000 Hz, which is a significant improvement over the current detectors. This design can also be applied to other types of sensors, including accelerometers and seismometers, which are also limited by the same noise sources as gravitational wave detectors. This design can also be realized using a sloshing cavity instead of a Michelson interferometer, which would provide a simpler design with the same level of sensitivity. This design can also be compared to other types of cavity-based sensors, including whispering gallery mode resonators and optomechanical resonators, to identify its unique features and areas of improvement. Recently, the eXtra-Large Multiple Input Multiple Output (XL-MIMO) technology has gained significant attention due to its potential to provide high security in beyond 5G networks. To investigate the feasibility of XL-MIMO in practice, we examine the visibility areas between different base station antennas in a stochastic access protocol. Our analysis reveals that there is no overlap in the visibility areas of adjacent antennas, which is contrary to the general assumption made in previous studies that considered these areas as overlapping. We further mathematically prove the non-overlapping condition by utilizing the pseudorange measurements. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering the accurate, non-overlapping visibility area condition in future XL-MIMO network studies. To demonstrate this, we conduct an examination of the stochastic access protocol's efficiency and find that it functions efficiently when the distance between the antennas is approximately three times their diameter. Our research suggests that future XL-MIMO network studies should utilize a more precise, non-overlapping visibility area model to ensure accurate predictions and recommendations. Our code is available online at \url{https://github.com/aliyaz/xl-mimo-sap}.

Measurements of high-energy muons that have traversered the Earth reveal the magnitude of the Earth's magnetic field within the core. By analyzing these muons, a precise assessment of the Earth's core magnetic field has been made, indicating a significant field strength of approximately 3.5 x 10^-5 Tesla. This finding is particularly notable as it surpasses the expectations of a neutrally charged core and suggests that the Earth's core must contain a substantial amount of protons. Estimates indicate that the core's proton density is roughly 10 times greater than previously thought, with estimates ranging from 10 to 30 times more. This enhanced proton density has implications for the Earth's core, potentially transforming it from a liquid iron-nickel core to a partially or fully solid state. This discovery also has far-reaching effects on the understanding of the Earth's thermal evolution, possibly altering the estimated age of the Earth by anywhere from 500 million to 1 billion years. Furthermore, this finding has significant implications for the study of large rotating magnetic objects, such as rotating neutron stars, and highlights the importance of considering magnetic stresses in the formation and evolution of these bodies. This research was made possible by a combination of underground muon detectors in Japan and the Grand Cherenkov Detector of the Tunka Advanced Mueller Scintillation Array in Russia. This discovery was also facilitated by advances in computing power and numerical methods, specifically the use of the MITgcm code to model the Earth's core and surrounding mantle. A key step for implementing quantum simulations and certain quantum computations involves efficiently generating a large number of identical, varying Fock states using Motlmer-Sorensen gates. In experiments based on trapped ions, this is particularly challenging due to the limited number of motional modes available and their strong coupling to each other. In such scenarios, where multiple modes are equally occupied, a modified Mølmer-Sørensen gate can provide equal contributions from each mode to produce a specific target Fock state in one of the modes. This leads to a range of possible gate implementations that can achieve the same outcome for different numbers of modes, thereby offering flexibility in experimental design. In particular, for a specific case with two modes, a frequency-stable gate can be achieved that maintains its stability even when its operating point coincides with a mode's coupling parameter, without compromising its effectiveness in generating a desired state. This is achieved by converting the mode-mode coupling into mode-field coupling in a beam of light, which can be easily modulated to achieve frequency stability. In experiments with two motional modes, this allows for the efficient generation of a range of Fock states with varying coherence, from a single-photon state that can serve as a channel for measurement-induced entanglement, to states with two photons that can facilitate the implementation of a Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. In contrast, traditional implementations would require precise adjustment of the number of applied gate cycles to match the number of modes, which becomes increasingly difficult with more modes. In the modified case, the number of gate cycles can be set to match the largest mode's coupling parameter, which in experiments with two modes can be as little as 1 cycle, and in more complex setups can reduce the number of required classical computational resources. In the specific example of two modes, the gate duration can be optimized to achieve a target state with a 99% success rate in just 2 cycles, which in turn allows for the generation of a range of states with 2, 3, 4, or more photons, as well as states with varying coherence, by simply adjusting the duration of the time a specific target Fock state remains available. In particular, this allows for the efficient creation of a state with 4 photons in one mode, which in turn can facilitate a 4-bit Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm, in just 4 cycles. In certain transition metal dichalcogenides like PdSe2 and PdTe2, due to unique interlayer bonding, a distinct "strongly linked" band structure forms, differing from conventional 2D and 3D materials. This results in an unusual, disentangled valence and conduction band structure near the Fermi level, lacking any kind of Dirac point, yet allowing for the creation of highly stable and open Fermi surfaces. As a consequence, these materials exhibit exceptional electrical conductivity and robustness against corrosion, making them suitable for high-performance applications in harsh environments. A theoretical framework is established to predict the strong interlayer bonding effect in Pd-based dichalcogenides by integrating ab-initio calculations with interlayer coupling analysis. This framework is applied to identify key factors contributing to the stability of the strongly linked state, revealing that the unique geometry of Pd atoms and their surrounding ligands are responsible for the large overlap between their d-orbitals, and thus facilitating the formation of a wide, open and stable band structure. This is further supported by the findings of similar band structures in other Pd-based compounds like PtSe2 and PtTe2. This study demonstrates that the strong interlayer coupling in Pd-based dichalcogenides can be controlled by adjusting the lattice parameters, and that it leads to the creation of a "hidden" 3D Dirac state in PdS2 and PdSe2, characterized by multiple Dirac points along the high symmetry lines of the 3D Brillouin zone, and located near the Fermi level. This results in the formation of intricate Fermi surface topologies, comprising multiple hypercubes and tetrahedrons, and may give rise to exotic quantum phenomena such as the formation of Weyl points and Fermi arcs along certain high-symmetry lines and surfaces. This hidden Dirac state can be further manipulated by applying external pressures, which causes a Peierls distortion and leads to the formation of a 1D chain of Dirac points along the c-axis in PdSe2, and results in the creation of a 1D or 2D Fermi surface in PdS2 and PdTe2. This study highlights the unique electronic properties of Pd-based dichalcogenides, and demonstrates that these materials can be tailored to exhibit a "hidden" 3D Dirac state, making them suitable for a wide range of applications, from quantum technology to catalysis. Neural language models have gained significant attention recently, yet a fundamental aspect of language modeling, namely n-gram models, has been largely overlooked. In our research, we explore the potential of neural networks as a data generator with n-gram models serving as an initial estimate. By formulating the task as a regression around the n-gram predictions, we found that using a simple neural network with a linear layer yielded superior results compared to transformer-based architectures. Our findings also indicate that employing a BPE-based subword representation can further improve performance. We believe this approach can be beneficial for generating specific text styles or for filling in missing text segments. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangliu/NgramIsBack.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a complex task, particularly when the quality of input images is compromised. This challenge is compounded for sequences of images, where face appearances can change significantly over time. To address this issue, our proposed method, the Self-Aligned Dual Face Prediction Network (SADRNet), is an end-to-end, sequential face reconstruction framework that simultaneously predicts three-dimensional face structures and texture images. This framework consists of two cascading networks: an initial face prediction network generates an aligned face structure and a corresponding texture image, while a second network refines the face structure and texture image based on the previously generated face features. Through extensive evaluation on two datasets, the CMU Pan-African Face and the ATR Face Database, along with the widely used FacePAK dataset for face reconstruction evaluation, our method achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art approaches in terms of reconstruction accuracy, as measured by mean absolute error and peak signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, our method demonstrates improved robustness and efficiency in reconstructing faces from low-quality images and sequences. With its ability to segment the input image into face and background regions, our method also offers a face reconstruction from scratch functionality without an initial face mask. A labeled ordered tree is defined as a tree with nodes labeled from a well-ordering, together with a left-child partial order. Letting $f_n$ denote the number of deepest vertices in labeled ordered trees of $n$ nodes, we derive an explicit formula for $f_n$ by analyzing recursive structures of the trees. By examining the deepest part of the trees, we identify two main components – a set of deepest root nodes and a set of child nodes to all deepest root nodes – which allows us to express $f_n$ as a sum of values of earlier $f_n$ and $C_n$ for $0 \leq n \leq 23$, with additional cases for $f_0, f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4, f_5, f_6, f_7, f_8, f_9, f_{10}, f_{11}, f_{12}, f_{13}, f_{14}, f_{15}, f_{16}, f_{17}, f_{18}, f_{19}, f_{20}, f_{21}, f_{22}, f_{23}$. Furthermore, we establish recursive relations to calculate $f_n$ for $n > 23$. We also examine the generating function $f(x)$ associated with the sequence $f_n$, from which we obtain insights into the enumerated sequence. Specifically, we find that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the derivative of the generating function associated with the sequence $C_n$, with an adjustment for an infinite series of negative terms. By analyzing this relationship, we identify connections to the gamma function and the Eulerian numbers. Finally, we establish connections between the enumerated sequence $f_n$ and another sequence defined by the number of nodes in the rightmost path of a random ordered tree of $n$ nodes, demonstrating that the number of deepest nodes in an ordered tree of $n$ nodes equals the number of nodes in the rightmost path of an ordered tree of $n$ nodes minus one, for $1 \leq n \leq 23$. For larger values of $n$, we provide an alternative description of the enumerated sequence $f_n$ based on the number of nodes in the rightmost path of a random ordered tree of $n$ nodes. A simplified global circulation model is used to simulate various large-scale atmospheric circulation regimes in a rotating frame with a horizontal Rayleigh friction term and thermal forcing. This model allows for the exploration of atmospheric circulation in simplified forms, from highly rotating and fast-moving systems to slower and more complex movements. In this study, we examine and compare the atmospheric circulation patterns in a rotating frame with different rotation rates, friction levels, and temperature gradients. As the rotation rate and friction level change, the circulation patterns transition between highly asymmetric, slow-moving and fast-moving regimes. We establish the existence and distinctness of minimizing surfaces with given boundary data in the category of submanifolds in a metric space, extending a significant result by Morsteeg and Preston to new homotopy scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that near any point of non-minimality, there is a local variation functional whose Jacobian coincides with the inclusion of the tangent space of surfaces that are not locally minimizing. This latter finding builds upon a crucial result of the same type, initially proven by a different method by a separate researcher. Both of these conclusions can be achieved under the assumption of a relatively mild topological property requiring surfaces to be path-connected. Filling in some essential background information, we also discuss some related results about the compactness of minimizing surfaces in metric spaces. Lastly, we examine specific examples in Euclidean spaces, showcasing situations in which there are infinitely many distinct minimizing surfaces with given boundary data in $R^n$. These examples also demonstrate the utility of a topological invariant known as Betti numbers in analyzing the variety of minimizing surfaces in Euclidean spaces. One of the main challenges in hyperparameter tuning for machine learning models is managing the trade-off between model performance and generality. A common method for finding optimal hyperparameters is using grid search with cross-validation, yet this approach often overestimates the effectiveness of the best hyperparameters found due to the variance inherent in cross-validation. This bias and its accompanying variance hinder the generalizability of the optimal hyperparameters discovered. In this paper, we investigate the impact of different cross-validation methods' variance on hyperparameter tuning, specifically exploring the effects of 5-fold, 10-fold, and J-K fold cross validation. Our findings reveal that the variance of these methods can be quite substantial, with 10-fold cross validation exhibiting notably high variance. In response to this discovery, we propose using J-K fold cross validation with an odd number of folds, specifically 9, as it yields significantly lower variance while maintaining computational efficiency. Our recommendations can be applied to various machine learning models, including text classification using BERT. Our code is available online for public review and replication. In addition to this code, we provide an illustrative example utilizing the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset. Our results demonstrate that, for example with this dataset using the BERT base model, the variance of the average CV score is approximately 0.046, whereas the variance of the best hyperparameter found is approximately 0.021. Our findings suggest that hyperparameter tuning with 9-fold cross validation yields a more reliable estimate of the model's performance, with a consequent improvement in the models' generalizability. Our research highlights the significance of accounting for the variance of cross-validation when evaluating the performance of machine learning models, with implications for the broader field of machine learning. Our approach to addressing this issue can be applied to various contexts, including, but not limited to, natural language processing. Our research also underscores the value of exploring different cross-validation methods' variance in the specific context of natural language processing, with the potential for new insights to be gained from this analysis. Our results further indicate that the variance of the average CV score is significantly greater than the variance of the best hyperparameter found, with implications for the development of more effective hyperparameter tuning strategies. Our research also highlights the potential for the hyperparameter tuning process to be more efficiently conducted by prioritizing the exploration of hyperparameters settings with low variance rather than those with high model performance. From improving language skills to resolving complex mathematical problems, artificial neural networks through reinforcement learning can acquire new knowledge when interacting with a trained neural network, typically referred to as an 'instructor' or 'teacher' and a 'pupil' or'student' respectively. The framework that facilitates this knowledge acquisition is known as an 'educator-pupil' framework. Since the introduction of this concept, numerous variations of the educator-pupil framework have emerged, with various names such as student-teacher, teacher-student, and knowledge distillation, although they all pertain to the same category. This survey aims to explore the diverse range of educator-pupil methods, with a focus on classification problems and deep neural networks. We examine the various ways the educator-pupil framework can be structured, the objectives that guide the learning process, and the applications of this framework in computer vision and beyond. With over 70 relevant publications included in this survey, we anticipate it will serve as a comprehensive and accessible introduction to the educator-pupil framework for both seasoned researchers and newcomers to this field.

Our proposed method, referred to as Brief Function Description (BFD), streamlines the efficient computation of Most Probable Explanations (MPE) and constrained optimization in graphical models by significantly reducing the time spent on likelihood computation. BFD achieves this improvement by condensing the function descriptions, which represent the set of unvisited variables and their corresponding potentials, from a potential-based representation to a vector-based one. This change enables faster comparison and combination of potentials, leading to a notable acceleration in the computation of MPE and constrained optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that BFD outperforms the Fast-Sweep-Approximate-Marginal (FSAM) algorithm and exhibits superior performance in various scenarios, including the computation of MPE, constrained optimization, and multi-objective optimization. The enhanced BFD algorithm also offers a more precise approximation of the exact solution, with an adjustable trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. The code for the BFD algorithm is openly accessible on GitHub. The proposed method offers a concise depiction of functions that accelerates the computation of MPE and constrained optimization in graphical models, presenting a valuable contribution to the field. Recoil effects from the interaction of light with matter have significant implications for high-accuracy absorption measurements, particularly when utilizing narrow resonances. As a result, it is crucial to consider how photon interactions influence the absorption coefficient's apparent value, especially in scenarios involving a forward-facing light beam. Here, we investigate the impact of recoil in a model of a strontium gas absorption against a background of fluorescent atoms, utilizing a numerical method to simulate the scenario. Here, we outline a general framework for examining this problem with a focus on the specific case of a strontium gas. In this context, we find that when the width of the light beam is much larger than the absorption length, the apparent absorption coefficient is influenced by a factor that depends on the light beam's characteristics and absorption properties, rather than the properties of the gas. Furthermore, when the light beam's width is comparable to the absorption length, we can no longer treat the light beam as a plane wave, and a new resonance window emerges in the limit of a thin light beam. This new resonance occurs when the light beam's diameter is equal to the absorption length and is characterized by a depth that is less than the depth of the original resonance. Notably, this new resonance is independent of the light's frequency and is solely determined by the light beam's properties. Here, we also discuss the specific case of an ultracold strontium gas, including a discussion of the effects of Doppler broadening and a numerical calculation of the new resonance window. In this scenario, we find that the new resonance can be either broader or narrower than the original resonance, and that the condition for the new resonance to be observable can be met with a sufficiently low temperature and a sufficiently narrow light beam. In the context of a Rb-Doppler-free absorption experiment, we found that the new resonance could be made narrower than the original resonance with a temperature of around 1 microKelvin and a light beam with a diameter of around 10 micrometers. Our research delves into the sudden, drastic transitions that suspensions experience under intense shear stress, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing data and innovative scaling approaches, our findings reveal a distinct, universal path in the phase diagram of shear thickening, influenced by both shear stress and particle collision energy. By applying a novel, robust method to extract exponents from multiple datasets, our study determines two key scaling regimes that reflect the disparate behaviors of low and high-concentration suspensions. The resulting insights provide a foundation for further theoretical exploration of shear thickening's underlying mechanisms. Our research focuses on suspensions composed of polyethylene glycol (PEG) particles, but the scaling framework presented is adaptable to other systems of soft, frictionless particles subject to collisional interactions. Our study highlights the importance of considering both shear stress and energy from particle collisions when defining the phase diagram of shear thickening. Our findings also demonstrate that the scaling exponents for low and high-concentration suspensions differ, with the latter exhibiting an exponent of 1.33 in the high-concentration regime. Web search engines like Google provide personalized results based on users' search history and account information, potentially leading to a significant amount of relevant information being concealed from users. This study investigates the extent to which this personalization results in overlooked pertinent information by analyzing the diversity of search results and their corresponding webpage contents. A controlled user study involving 20 participants was conducted to assess their ability to identify relevant documents from a pool of 20, with half of the documents being concealed due to personalization. The results showed that an average of 4.5 relevant documents were hidden from participants by Google's algorithm, with a standard deviation of 2.3. Furthermore, a separate analysis of 150 concealed and 150 visible search result pages revealed that the former contained 12% fewer relevant contents, on average. These findings are significant because they quantify the potential consequences of web search personalization, highlighting the potential risks to users who rely on incomplete information. This research has implications for search engine optimization practices, as well as for users who need to account for the limitations of their search results. Finally, the study suggests potential areas for improvement in search engines, such as providing users with more transparent information about the diversity of their search results. Leveraging a combination of data-driven and model-based strategies, this method utilizes continuous data acquisition during free breathing. By reconstructing images using a low-resolution initial estimate and iteratively refining them with a model that accounts for motion, this approach achieves high-quality results. A key challenge in efficient paired-permutation testing arises from the difficulty in pinpointing the specific permutations that correspond to observed distribution shifts, particularly when testing hypotheses about structured or correlated data. To address this issue, we develop an efficient algorithm for determining the precise set of permutations that exhibit the same pattern of distribution differences as observed in paired data. This achievement is made possible by representing paired permutations as sequences of permutations in independent variables, which allows us to leverage fast permutation methods while preserving statistical efficiency. Our algorithm is particularly beneficial for addressing common problems such as testing for symmetry in dependent data, detecting clusters with different distribution characteristics, and determining the order of correlated time-series data. Our numerical experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency over existing random sampling approaches. Our algorithm is implemented in the RPADataTools package for R.

A comprehensive dataset of the container shipping industry has been assembled from 1966 to 2009, encompassing five key variables: freight rates, new ship prices, secondhand ship prices, scrap prices, and shipping volume. This dataset provides a unique opportunity for analysis and modeling, particularly in addressing the industry's inherent challenges and complexities. Notably, the dataset includes a previously unexplored period of significant crisis, from 1999 to 2004, characterized by unprecedented market fluctuations and substantial losses. By examining this crisis, researchers can gain valuable insights into industry dynamics and patterns of behavior. The dataset is now available for public use and can be accessed through the MIT Center for Engineering Systems Advances through Mathematics website. It is hoped that this resource will facilitate collaborative research among the academic community, industry professionals, and shipping companies. The dataset consists of annual freight rate, shipping volume, new ship price, secondhand ship price, and scrap price data for the industry as a whole, as well as separate figures for six different ship types. The analysis of this data can be carried out using various tools and techniques, including regression analysis, time series modeling, control theory, and game theory. The research team invites suggestions and ideas from interested parties on how to proceed with the analysis of this dataset. The associated code and data are available at https://cesam.mit.edu/research/industry-dynamics/container-shipping. The concept of fabric spaces, initially introduced by Harvey to generalize the idea of regular cell complexes, is utilized to create a framework that encompasses changing simplicial complexes. This framework is particularly useful in modeling geometric transformations, such as simplicial surface flows, folding, unfolding, and folding/unfolding operations, which alter the simplicial complex of an embedded surface. By examining specific examples with triangulated tori, we demonstrate how this framework can model complex transformations resulting from multiple flow/folding/unfolding operations. Furthermore, this framework provides a theoretical foundation for the concept of "simplicial surface flows" and offers a method for constructing such flows from folding/unfolding operations. This construction can be particularly useful in visualizing and analyzing specific flow trajectories. Additionally, this framework offers a means of determining whether a surface defined by a simplicial complex can be smoothly deformed into another surface defined by a different simplicial complex, achieved by examining the flow between their respective simplicial complexes. This examination is made possible by the introduction of a new graph structure called the "simplicial graph of a surface", which encodes the information about the surface's simplicial complex and can be utilized to determine whether two surfaces can be smoothly deformed into each other. This graph structure can also be used to determine whether a surface can be smoothly deformed into a specific surface defined by a simplicial complex, as well as to find the shortest flow that deforms the first surface into the second. This can be particularly useful in the study of geometric rigidity and flexibility. This study is an extension of an earlier work by the same author, published as arXiv:2111.07442. To explore the potential of future $e^+e^-$ colliders in discovering new physics through Beyond the Standard Model Higgs interactions during Higgs pair production, this study utilizes Effective Field Theories to simulate double Higgs boson creation in such a context. Specifically, we examine the ability of these colliders, with energy options of 250 GeV and 300 GeV, to detect Higgs interactions involving leptoquarks, scalar and vector quark triplets, and to what extent they can reveal specific properties of these interactions. Our analysis focuses on the production of neutral Higgs pairs and considers both the production of light and heavy neutral Higgs bosons. We investigate different energy configurations for the colliders, as well as various effective Higgs couplings, to identify the most promising conditions for discovering new Higgs interactions. Our findings suggest that at an energy of 250 GeV, the detection of new Higgs interactions may be limited to specific modes of pair production, whereas at 300 GeV multiple modes become accessible. We also examine the potential for these colliders to distinguish between different new Higgs interactions by analyzing the cross-sections of different pair production modes. Our results indicate that, with the ability to measure luminosity, polarisation, and Lorentz boost, future $e^+e^-$ colliders can differentiate between various new Higgs interactions, although the level of distinction varies with energy and particle masses. Our study concludes by exploring the prospects for discovering new Higgs interactions at $e^+e^-$ colliders with higher energies, finding that an energy of 240 GeV is sufficient to discover leptoquark interactions, while energies of 260 GeV and 280 GeV are required to discover scalar and vector quark interactions respectively. We also provide recommendations for optimising the operating energy of these colliders to enhance the discovery of new Higgs interactions. We have an explicit and general formulation to determine local Lagrangians for gravity within the framework of metric variations. Our approach applies to general relativistic theories and identifies key components required for a Lagrangian description. The anisotropic drag force experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material is a complex and poorly understood phenomenon. Despite its significance in various settings, including sand, mud, and snow, the underlying causes of anisotropic drag have not been fully explored. Previous studies have attributed the anisotropy to the object's orientation and the presence of lateral stress within the granular material. However, these explanations are not universally accepted and more research is needed to validate them. In an attempt to shed light on this issue, we conducted a series of experiments using a cylindrical object of varying lengths in a fluid-saturated granular bed. By analyzing the drag forces acting on the object from both its front and side, we found that the anisotropic drag coefficient is indeed influenced by the object's orientation but not significantly so. On the other hand, we found little evidence to support the idea that lateral stress contributes to the anisotropy. Instead, our findings suggest that the anisotropy may arise from the object's interaction with specific granular layers, particularly those formed by the settling of sediment. This hypothesis is supported by observations of the object's tracks and sediment layers and is consistent with the anisotropy observed in natural sedimentary environments. This discovery highlights the importance of considering the object's interaction with local sediment structures when modeling drag forces in such settings. Understanding organ deformation through biomechanical modeling is crucial in medical procedures such as surgical interventions and image-guided therapies. To enhance the effectiveness of these methods, it is essential to develop efficient and accurate biomechanical models that can be easily scaled to various applications. In the context of abdominal organ modeling during laparoscopy, it's vital to integrate biomechanical models with visual data. However, creating these models from scratch can be time-consuming and impractical for real-time use cases. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages a library of pre-existing models to create a data-driven biomechanical framework for aligning soft tissues. This approach enables us to generate a biomechanical model that can be easily matched to a target organ by utilizing a narrow set of surface features. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by developing a simplified lung model and applying it to a real-world dataset. Furthermore, we show that our model can be effectively utilized for tracking organ deformation over time. To evaluate our model's accuracy in a more realistic scenario, we conducted an experiment on a publicly available dataset, resulting in an average alignment error of 4.5mm. Our data-driven biomechanical framework provides a versatile tool for various medical applications, including image-guided interventions and surgical simulations.
