An astrometric mission like Gaia, with high-precision measurements of stellar positions, will be extremely sensitive to variations in gravitational acceleration. This is reflected in the limited accuracy of PPN $\gamma$ determinations from Gaia data, with an expected uncertainty of 0.0001. We have examined the impact of this uncertainty on parallax measurements, finding that it will result in an added error of approximately 0.0001*sqrt(1/μ) for main-sequence stars with effective temperatures between 4000 and 7000 K, where $\mu$ is the stellar mass in solar masses. This translates to a mean added error of around 0.0006 in parallax measurements for a mass distribution that follows a Salpeter law. However, for lower-mass stars (with masses less than 0.5 solar masses), the effect is more pronounced, with added parallax errors exceeding 0.01. This highlights the significance of refining PPN $\gamma$ through other means, such as using data from gravitational waves detected by LIGO. This research has implications for future astrometric missions with even higher precision, such as Gaia's enhanced version Gaia+, and similar missions like JAXA's AST3-2 and AST3-3. It also underscores the importance of accurately determining the gravitational constant G, with an expected uncertainty of around 10^-4 for Gaia data, and the need for precise measurements of the relativistic precession of the perihelion of Mercury's orbit. This will also enable the direct determination of PPN $\gamma$ from Gaia data, without relying on external estimates of G. A systematic examination of cometary spectra involving molecular cations has revealed a gap in knowledge. Despite the vast amount of data collected by spacecraft, particularly by the Rosetta's COSIMA and VLT/CRISS instruments during the Comet 67P/Chodorkin-Gerlach observations, there are significant gaps in the available spectral measurements for some of these molecular cations, particularly those containing oxygen. A comprehensive analysis of existing spectra has been compared to laboratory measurements, revealing that about 70% of the measured cometary spectral features associated with molecular oxygen cations are based on assumptions, as the underlying laboratory spectra are incomplete. This knowledge deficiency affects the analysis of cometary data, specifically with regards to the distribution of molecular oxygen cations, and highlights the need for more comprehensive laboratory spectral references, as well as additional measurements from future comet missions. This issue is particularly relevant for the COSIMA instrument, which has a limited spectral resolution that may not adequately account for some of the laboratory spectral features. This problem also affects other similar instruments, such as the IONASA on board the Tianwen-1 mission, and highlights the importance of accurate laboratory spectral databases for the interpretation of future cometary data. A common challenge in medical image segmentation arises from the significant disparity between large amounts of unlabelled images and limited expert-labeled training data. To tackle this issue, various semi-supervised methods have been developed to utilize unannotated medical images by constraining the difference between predicted and observed values. In response to the growing interest in such techniques, researchers have explored innovative ways to incorporate consistency regularization to enhance model performance. This study presents an alternative simple approach to enhance the effectiveness of semi-supervised image segmentation models by promoting their adherence to known characteristics. In particular, we leverage a previously established property of medical images to create a simple yet effective evaluation metric. By incorporating this measure into a standard training procedure through L2 minimization, we demonstrate a significant improvement in segmentation accuracy in both brain and abdominal scan analyses. Compared to existing methods, our approach shows a notable 5.3% improvement in the Dice score for the brain study and a 7.5% increase for the abdominal study. This research highlights the value of leveraging intrinsic properties of medical images to develop targeted evaluation metrics that can be used to enhance segmentation performance through simple and efficient means. This approach can be applied to various medical image segmentation tasks beyond the specific examples presented here. This study is an invitation to explore the potential of intrinsic image properties for guiding segmentation performance through various means, including consistency regularization. The behavior of individual atoms within a solid can be significantly influenced by their local environment, and understanding these interactions is crucial for developing and improving materials. By applying graph neural networks to simulate the quantum mechanics of these interactions, we were able to accurately model the energy levels of atoms within a 2D material with high precision. Furthermore, by utilizing a simple and interpretable model, we were able to analyze the key factors contributing to fluctuations in energy levels, revealing the presence of chaotic dynamics that drives random variations in energy levels. Verifying our findings, we compared our results to precise quantum simulations, and also explored how material properties change over time according to Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, a key indicator of chaotic dynamics. Our framework provides a flexible tool for studying the dynamics of individual atoms within a solid. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quantum-Computing-Group/PyTorch-QC.

Given any complex variety 'X' and a fixed Hilbert space 'H', we define a collection of holomorphic functions on 'X' with values in 'H'. This set, denoted by 'O(X,H)', forms a module over the polynomial ring 'O(X)'. Within this context, we investigate the properties of 'O(X,H)' when 'X' is not compact. Specifically, for an analyst's compactification 'X' of 'X', we examine when the natural map from 'O(X,H)$ to O(X,H)$ is surjective, including instances where this map fails to be surjective. This failure occurs when 'X' has infinitely many generic irreducible components. Additionally, we show that the span of 'O(X,H)$ forms a dense subspace of 'C^0(X,H)$ when 'X' has no generic irreducible components. This result extends a previous finding by Bertrand-Hacquard. Notably, this extension is achieved without relying on the assumption of analytic continuation for polynomial functions. Lastly, we provide a local characterization of the span of 'O(X,H)$, enabling an exploration of this span through local analytic properties. This local analysis reveals that the span of 'O(X,H)$ remains dense within 'C^0(X,H)$, provided 'X' possesses no isolated points in its closure. This study builds upon the work presented in a previous paper by the same authors, titled: A Characterization of the Span of Holomorphic Functions on Varieties. This earlier research established a necessary and sufficient condition for the span of 'O(X,H)$ to be equal to 'C^0(X,H)$ when 'X' is compact. This current paper extends this earlier result to non-compact varieties by introducing an equivalent definition of the span of 'O(X,H)$, allowing a characterization of this span for arbitrary varieties. This definition and its associated characterization involve the concept of a specific subset of 'X', denoted by 'V_H$, which is formed by the points at which the absolute value of 'f$ exceeds 1 for all 'f$ in 'O(X,H)$. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly slow down the process. Our proposed method, unDelayed, streamlines this process by allowing unbounded gradient accumulation across devices. This approach ensures that the gradient norm remains bounded, a prerequisite for many optimizers. We demonstrate that under mild assumptions, the norm of accumulated gradients will eventually be limited. Our experiments show that unDelayed yields faster training and comparable test accuracy to the traditional synchronized approach. Our findings suggest that unDelayed can be an efficient and effective choice for various optimizers and complex models in cross-device federated learning. Recent advancements in end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have led to improved performance, yet the need for vast amounts of training data remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, ASR systems are being developed for multi-language transfer, where a single model can process multiple languages. However, evaluating and comparing such systems across different languages is difficult due to varying dataset availability and data quality. In this work, we explore a transfer learning approach using a sequence of models with increasing linguistic complexity, starting from a simple model for low-resource languages and gradually incorporating more complex models for higher-resource languages. Our experiments with multi-language transfer on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate a 4.3% relative improvement in the WER when using a cascade of two models. Furthermore, we show that a similar approach can be applied across languages with a 13.6% relative WER reduction when transferring from a low-resource language to a high-resource language with a different script. These findings support further exploration of the proposed cascade transfer learning method as a standard evaluation protocol for ASR systems is yet to be established. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/EsraGundogdu/PyTorch-ASR-Cascade.

We have derived a new second-order approximation for a static and spherically symmetric relativistic objects composed of two fluids under the nonisotropic pressure assumption. This approximation is particularly relevant for objects with distinct cores and mantles, such as proto-neutron stars. We have further developed a numerical method to solve for objects made of two fluids with varying pressure properties. Our analysis reveals that the (Ω, P) phase diagram can exhibit multiple branches for each central density. Our nonrelativistic counterpart shows that the phase diagram can have three branches: a lower branch representing a purely hydrostatic configuration, a middle branch representing a collapsed state in mass-shedding, and an upper branch representing a rotating fluid with constant entropy. Notably, our results differ from those obtained using the adiabatic index, which only yields two branches. Our numerical approach also allows for the modeling of objects with sharp interfaces by adjusting the pressure properties. We have further validated our numerical method against these results. Our approximation and numerical method can be applied to a wide range of objects, from compact stars to supermassive black holes, and we have tested our code by modeling such objects. We have also compared our results with those obtained using the Buchdahl criterion and the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation of state, and we have found that our numerical method can reproduce the same phase diagrams. Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification methods focus on developing highly customized models for specific sources and target languages. However, this approach can lead to overfitting when source data is limited. To address this challenge, we explore the potential of meta-learning to enhance domain adaptability. Leveraging a single administration task that combines administration and evaluation on a single, distinct language pair, our results show significant improvements in domain transfer. Specifically, when transferring from a source data set consisting of 5,000 sentence pairs for the English-to-Spanish pair, our model exhibits notable gains, with as much as 8 points in BLEU score and 0.7 points in F-score compared to the domain-specific model. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates robust performance under conditions with limited target data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in the IWSLT 2019 ESPETO TO ENGLISH machine translation task and the NAF GL Monroe test set. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenxiangulv/FET.

In a setting where agents with distinct values for items, expressed as integer multiples of a basic unit, engage in a combinatorial auction, we examine the existence and characteristics of pure Nash equilibria for various allocation rules. Specifically, we investigate whether there's a valuation structure for any given combinatorial auction that allows all value vectors to have a specific property - namely, being able to allocate fairly for at least one allocation rule. We also explore specific valuation scenarios, including graph-based allocations, where we can guarantee this property for all value vectors, as well as more general scenarios, such as matroid-based allocations, where this property holds only for some value vectors. Furthermore, we compare the fairness of all pure Nash equilibria to the fairness of the allocation that maximizes total value, with an approachable proof that relies on our previous research on the relationship between pure Nash equilibria and the allocation that maximizes total value. This comparison provides an insight into the trade-off between the efficiency of an auction and the fairness of its pure Nash equilibria for any combinatorial auction. This research extends our previous findings related to graph-based allocations and proportional allocation, as well as other valuation scenarios. Some of these results were previously presented at WAOA 2019, SAGT 2019, and EC 2019.

UGC 8839 is a peculiar galaxy that exhibits both spiral and disk-like features in the H-alpha emission, yet displays a prominent, highly ionized "halo" when using neutral atomic gas as the tracer. A new, high-resolution spectroscopic study using the VLT's MUSE reveals a highly extended, nearly circular "atmosphere" of 75 kiloparsecs in length, featuring a wide range of velocities that mirror the galaxy's rotation. This suggests that this "atmosphere" is likely a result of a massive, slow-moving accretion disk rather than a result of tidal forces or an active galactic nucleus. With a total mass estimated to be 10 to the power of 9 solar masses, this disk is significantly more massive than any known galaxy disk and raises interesting questions about how it formed and influenced the galaxy's evolution. Additionally, this finding challenges previous observations of the galaxy's neutral gas, revealing a much more massive, highly extended "dark" component that resembles a "dark disk" and may also be present in other galaxies. This discovery was made possible by the high sensitivity and resolution of the MUSE, and highlights the importance of using the neutral gas as a tracer for studying the structure of galaxies. This research also highlights the limitations of using emission lines alone to study the structure of distant galaxies. Using lattice QCD, a detailed investigation of the correlation between the two flavors of quarks within the pion was conducted. Based on a comprehensive study of various correlation functions, two-flavor correlations were quantified through two distinct measures: the average distance between quark and antiquark, and the probability distribution of these distances. Notable variations in these measures were observed between pions composed of up and anti-up quarks versus those composed of down and anti-down quarks. Furthermore, comparisons were made with previous lattice QCD findings for the correlations within the pion, and also with theoretical predictions based on chiral effective field theory. The results obtained from this study are now available in the public domain. The lattice approach employed relied on data from the improved Wilson quark action, with multiple pion-mass ratios studied across two different lattice spacings, with corresponding pion masses ranging from approximately 140 to 900 MeV. The corrections for finite volume effects were also assessed and found to be minimal. The lattice calculations were performed using the stout gauge link improvement for the lattice gluon field, with five different pion masses investigated for each of the two lattice spacings. The resulting correlation measures were then fitted to power-law distributions, with the fitted parameters subsequently compared across different pion masses and lattice spacings. The lattice data were obtained from the RBC and UKQCD Collaborations' existing simulations, with the volume used being approximately 4.5 fm in linear extent. The findings from this study are relevant to ongoing efforts to improve the accuracy of lattice calculations, specifically with regards to identifying suitable lattice spacings and volumes for future simulations. The discovery of a power-law distribution of two-flavor correlations within the pion, with an estimated average distance between quark and antiquark of approximately 0.6 fm, also provides a theoretical framework that may be applied to experimental observations of meson correlations. The availability of lattice data for the probability distribution of correlation distances may facilitate comparisons with non-lattice approaches, with the potential to assess the impact of finite volume effects and to improve the accuracy of these comparisons. The lattice data for the probability distribution of correlation distances may be accessed through the ILDG repository. The findings from this study are also relevant to ongoing efforts to improve the accuracy of calculations for light quark masses, specifically with regards to identifying suitable lattice spacings and volumes for future simulations. Evaluating accretion rates in young stellar objects is crucial for determining the mass distribution within these objects. However, measuring accretion rates is challenging due to the variability of accretion fluctuations, which can be influenced by different observation periods. Our previous research identified the one-year orbital period of variable accretion rates in the young T Tauri star XX Cha. By analyzing new data from the VOSPECT and the GIOUVELAGE spectrometers and photometric data from the K2 space telescope, we found that the accretion fluctuations in XX Cha are irregular and occur primarily during the star's periastron. This pattern causes a significant increase in the standard deviation of accretion rates at this time. By accounting for this orbital variation in our analysis, we reduced the standard deviation of accretion rates by a factor of five. This discovery highlights the importance of considering the unusual orbital pattern of XX Cha when studying accretion rates, and it also underscores the significance of long-term observations in accurately determining the standard deviation of accretion rates. Furthermore, this finding is relevant to studies using accretion rates to constrain the mass distribution of young stellar objects. Additionally, the unusual behavior of XX Cha may be an extreme example of a more general phenomenon observed in other T Tauri stars with orbital periods of a few days. This could be an indication that the distribution of mass within these objects is more complex and variable than previously thought. This hypothesis is supported by observations of the T Tauri star V929 Sco, which exhibits similar variability on a longer period of 11.4 years. This suggests that the distribution of mass within these objects may be dynamic and influenced by external forces, such as the gravitational pull of companion stars. This hypothesis is also consistent with the distribution of mass observed in the binary star system NY Ser. This is further discussed in an accompanying paper. This research also utilized the ESO/3.6m telescope at La Silla, Chile. This research also utilized the TESS mission, which is funded by NASA. To address challenges in offline learning for multiple agents, many models rely on centralised representation and shared policies. However, these approaches often fail when faced with scarcity of positive data trajectories. A new issue arises when multiple agents are involved, as different agents may act independently and simultaneously to achieve individual goals. This is particularly true in complex, realistic scenarios. To tackle these difficulties, we propose a novel individualised multi-agent framework based on separate policy networks for each agent. Each policy is trained to maximise individual rewards while considering interactions with other agents. To handle limited positive data, we develop a selective sampling approach that prioritises the most informative negative experience trajectories. This is combined with a transfer learning method for transferring knowledge between different data distributions. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. By applying our method to a realistic multiplayer game, we show that it is possible to transfer knowledge from a much simpler previous version of the game. Furthermore, our approach can leverage the benefits of negative experience data. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/PAVE. In particular, Federated Learning (FL) has shown considerable promise in this regard. FL enables multiple parties to collaborate on training a shared model without exchanging raw data, thus providing an efficient solution for addressing privacy and security concerns. FL-based protocols for various applications in IoVs, such as traffic prediction and management, have shown notable improvements in security and privacy. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova with a known nova eruption in 1966, has been observed in X-rays since 1994 but was not previously detected in gamma-rays until the nova eruption in 2020.  We used data from the Comprehensive Supergiant Enhanced X-ray Observation (CGSEX) and the all-sky gamma-ray monitor (TXES) to study the pre-eruption activity of V392 Persei.  V392 Persei's pre-eruption X-ray spectrum is similar to that of other novae, with a strong soft X-ray component likely caused by a massive accretion disk.  The pre-eruption X-ray luminosity of V392 Persei is average when compared to other novae, but its pre-eruption X-ray variability is unusually high when compared to other novae.  V392 Persei's pre-eruption X-ray spectrum is also similar to that of other dwarf novae during their outburst phase, suggesting that its pre-eruption X-ray properties are a result of its classification as a dwarf nova rather than any unique property.  We also detected a persistent gamma-ray emission component from V392 Persei during its eruption, which is a first for a nova.  The origin of the gamma-ray emission from V392 Persei is unclear but it could be the result of a high mass accretion rate during its eruption.  We also detected a hard X-ray tail during the eruption of V392 Persei, which is a first for a nova.  The X-ray and gamma-ray light curves of V392 Persei have different shapes, with the X-ray light curve peaking earlier than the gamma-ray light curve.  We also detected a long-lived accretion disk during the eruption of V392 Persei, which is a first for a nova.  The temperature of the white dwarf in V392 Persei is estimated to be around 80 eV based on the pre-eruption X-ray spectrum, which is a first for a nova.  V392 Persei is now in a quiescent state with a soft X-ray spectrum similar to that of other quiescent novae. Tuning the curvature of a two-dimensional lattice in the Hofstadter model leads to a hierarchy of nonequilibrium phenomena along the surface of a cylinder. Our simulations reveal that this results in diverse phases of motion, including areas with sturdy currents that defy equilibrium behavior. We found that sturdy currents can form in regions with specific Peierl's tilting parameters, such as around the center of the parameter space or at the edge of the lattice. These sturdy currents persist even when the curvature is small and can be distinguished from transient nonequilibrium phases. Our research also shows that sturdy currents can be driven by tilting the chemical potential or the curvature of the lattice. We identified the underlying physics of sturdy currents in terms of localized states that share properties with edge states and showed that they can be described using a one-dimensional model. Our findings in the Hofstadter model suggest that sturdy nonequilibrium phases may also appear in other models with localized states along a curved interface. Our research used numerical simulations with exact diagonalization and a matrix product unitary operator transformation.

Using 15 years of X-ray observations from the Chandra telescope, the rate of accretion of matter has been studied for a sample of supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies. By analyzing the light curves of 108 active galactic nuclei, researchers found that the rate at which matter is drawn into black holes, as indicated by their brightening or fading, ranges from very slowly to very quickly, but on average is about 0.025 times the Eddington limit. This rate is consistent across different galaxies with varying luminosity and it's also found that the rate of matter being pulled into black holes does not influence the rate of matter being pulled into their accretion disks. Additionally, by examining the light curves for signs of sudden, large-scale changes in the rate of accretion, the researchers set an upper limit on the rate of mass reduction due to Bondi mass accretion, which is a theoretical process by which the gravitational influence of a massive object is reduced as it moves away from a smaller object it was once attracting. Based on the analysis of 108 galaxies over a 15-year period, the researchers found that the average rate of mass reduction due to Bondi accretion is less than 0.0003 per year, which is a more stringent limit than previously known. This new limit provides a clearer understanding of the behavior of galaxies and offers a more precise benchmark for computer simulations of galaxy evolution. This research also highlights the value of long-term observations in studying the evolution of galaxies and offers insights into how galaxies grow and change over time. This study used a new method of analyzing light curves that takes into account the random fluctuations in X-ray brightness, which has not been used in similar research before. In this work, we present TextWorldExpress, a Python expression evaluator that executes text games 50 times faster than existing alternatives, allowing for the exploration of over one million steps per second.
By optimizing performance through multi-threading, function compilation, and memory optimization, we demonstrate significant speed improvements in several benchmark scenarios.
TextWorldExpress is an open-source tool available under the permissive Apache License 2.0.

Deep learning models, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved high accuracy in video recognition tasks but at the expense of significantly increased computational requirements compared to traditional methods. To address this issue, a novel LSTM model with a compact architecture was developed, characterized by a unique layer structure and a memory cell design that minimizes computational complexity while maintaining high recognition performance. The proposed design was specifically tailored for a particular video recognition dataset and did not provide a general framework. To make the design more versatile, the LSTM architecture was modified to a standard architecture, and the hardware implementation was adapted to accommodate this change. The resulting LSTM network achieved a high accuracy of 95.05% in the UCF-101 dataset with a significant reduction in computational cost. The energy-efficient LSTM hardware was designed using a Method-Hardware Co-Design (MHC) flow, which integrated the LSTM model with the hardware platform through multiple iterations. The hardware implementation utilized a Hierarchical Tucker Tensor Decomposition (HTTD) technique to reduce memory and register requirements, resulting in an energy-efficient design that consumed only 176.5K (32KB+144.5K bit) of memory. The LSTM network was trained on a compact version of the MNIST dataset with 5000 samples and achieved a classification accuracy of 95.3% with a low throughput of 1024 bits/ cycle and a low computation cost of 24.5 cycles/element. The hardware implementation can be scaled up to larger datasets by increasing the memory size, allowing for the classification of larger datasets. Given a real-valued function defined on a subset of natural numbers, we develop the prime decomposition approach to analyze its iterates. For a non-decreasing function with a finite number of values, we establish conditions under which the number of its iterates exhibited on a given natural number is smallest when the largest divisor of that number is mapped to its maximum value. Additionally, we identify all natural numbers whose largest divisor is mapped to its maximum value by the square of the $n$th prime function. Furthermore, we examine how the distribution of natural numbers mapped to their maximum value by this square function relates to the distribution of primes. Lastly, we explore connections to the Erdős-Selberg method for counting prime numbers.

Saturn's polar atmosphere undergoes significant changes with the seasons, reflecting the planet's substantial axial tilt. During its approach to summer, a temporary polar vortex forms over each pole before dissipating with equinox, and research suggests this phenomenon is caused by temperature differences resulting from seasonally varying solar radiation. Although Saturn's polar atmosphere is generally inaccessible due to dense clouds of sulfur and ice, astronomers have been able to study this phenomenon by observing mid-infrared spectra emanating from the upper levels of Saturn's atmosphere. The newly found vortex exhibits unique spectral features, and its formation likely results from the interaction between atmospheric waves and the temperature gradients near the poles. Instead, it suggests that the hexagonal pattern at the poles may be more resilient than previously believed, and that the same region of Saturn's atmosphere can host multiple vortices simultaneously. The study of the northern vortex's chemical composition has also revealed that it contains less ethane than its southern counterpart, which may be related to the differing solar radiation the two poles receive during their respective summers. The findings presented here are based on data collected between 2005 and 2017 but are likely to be limited in duration, as they were influenced by the changing orbital positions of Saturn and its largest moon, Titan. The discovery of these vortices in the Saturnian atmosphere during its summer season highlights the significance of continued observation of this phenomenon, which may be affected by the changing solar radiation and the resulting temperature gradients. Discourse markers like "however" play a significant role in conveying the intended meaning of text, particularly in enhancing the clarity of contrasts. Despite their significance, many current NLP methods overlook these markers or misunderstand their implications. To address this limitation, we present a statistical approach to assign semantic functions to common contrastive discourse markers, testing the method's effectiveness with a novel evaluation framework. The results show that our statistical approach accurately infers the semantic functions of these markers in a majority of cases. To further refine the method, we explore extensions to the model, leading to an improvement in performance. To facilitate reproducibility, the code and data used in this research are made available in an accompanying repository. This research provides a foundation for exploring the complex relationships between discourse markers, grammatical structure, and semantic meaning. This research is relevant to the broader NLP community, particularly in areas like semantic analysis, parsing, and sentence interpretation. This research also provides an opportunity for future investigation into the various ways discourse markers influence the semantics of sentences, including conjunction, conditionality, and contrast. We investigate the global landscape of a broad class of matrix decomposition problems subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint. This leads to a geodesic convex optimization problem when the objective function is composed of a convex part of the Euclidean norm and the Frobenius norm. In a general case, where the number of decomposition components equals the matrix size, we find that the presence of a large number of sharp edges in the support of the solution matrix leads to a nonconvex landscape with multiple local minima. However, when the size of the decomposition components is much smaller than the matrix size, we demonstrate that the optimization problem becomes geodesically convex, featuring a single local minimum, and we provide an estimate for its depth. This is further illustrated with an example from multishielded portfolio optimization. Finally, we discuss how our findings can be related to existing results on the convexity of matrix optimization problems. A key problem in graph theory, identifying whether every cubic bipartite graph can be converted into a Hamiltonian cycle by removing edges, has been an open and challenging question. In 1999, a proposed proof for a specific class of bipartite graphs, named "right-angled" or "Hamiltonian" graphs, was disputed, leaving the general case unsolved. Another related and more specific question, concerning edge-tinting of these graphs, has also been unresolved. This paper provides a specific counterexample to both of these unknown cases – finding an edge that must be included in every Hamiltonian cycle of the graph G=K3,ṩ3, and also failing to find a Hamiltonian cycle in the reduced graph, thus settling the dispute over the previous incorrect proof. This counterexample specifically excludes the simpler edge-tinting result for which a different, much simpler proof was found in 2020. This counterexample has many notable features including being non-vertex-transitive, containing an abelian group of automorphisms of type symmetric, and possessing many other unique properties. This paper also outlines the search methods used to find the counterexample, and suggests potential future research directions. This particular counterexample was found using a computer-assisted search, and due to its complex nature, multiple different methods were required to validate its properties. This paper concludes by noting that the methods used to find and verify this counterexample are likely to be useful for tackling the more general edge-tinting problem. A key challenge in studying the evolution of games through co-evolution is addressing the requirement for precise type representations. This issue is particularly pronounced when considering the convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Our research addresses this concern by introducing a novel approach to co-evolution based on type changes, which can be viewed as a combination of the Clausius-Darwin-Von Neumann (CDN) cycle. This framework enables the exploration of games' evolution at both a population and individual level. It also provides a means to examine the types of dynamics that can arise, including convergence to a Nash Equilibrium, coexistence, and the emergence of complex structures. Our approach is particularly effective for examining the local dynamics of games' evolution, which can be represented as a web of interacting valleys and mountains of the type space. Our research involves applying this framework to re-analyzing previous numerical and analytical results from the study of a linear Cournot model, as well as to the introduction of a new model, the circular Cournot model. Our findings from these analyses demonstrate that the repetition of the CDN cycle can lead to the creation of periodic attractors, which can result in the maintenance of complex patterns of variation and the delay of convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Our research highlights the value of this co-evolutionary approach in providing insights into the types of dynamics that can arise in games' evolution, and the importance of considering the effects of type changes and the resulting valleys and mountains of the type space. Our findings are relevant to a broad range of contexts, from economics to biology, and our approach can be applied to the study of any context that involves the evolution of strategies among symmetric agents. Our research also involves suggesting a new method for determining the types of dynamics that can arise in games' evolution, which can be achieved by reconstructing the valleys and mountains of the type space from numerical data. Our research further involves exploring the relationship between this new method and other existing approaches to analyzing the types of dynamics that can arise in games' evolution, and our findings from this analysis provide insights into the limitations of the existing approaches and the conditions under which they can accurately capture the types of dynamics that can arise in games' evolution. Our research also involves examining the effects of changing the size of the type space on the types of dynamics that can arise in games' evolution, and our findings from this analysis demonstrate that the repetition of the CDN cycle can lead to the creation of complex structures of the type space, which can result in the delay of convergence to a Nash Equilibrium.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We aim to investigate the properties of the symbolic and normal powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$. Specifically, we seek to determine conditions under which the $mth$ symbolic power of $I(\mathcal{D})$ equals its radical, and we establish relationships between the normal and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$. Additionally, we examine the containment of the powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ within the containment of the powers of its vertex ideal, providing an example that showcases the non-equality of these containments. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the depth of the powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ and provide an alternative formula for calculating the depth of the normal powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$. These findings generalize the results obtained for edge ideals of undirected graphs by some of the authors in their prior work. Moreover, we derive specific conditions that guarantee the equality of the depth of the normal and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$, and we show that the depth of the normal powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ is greater than or equal to the minimum of the number of vertices and the number of edges in $\mathcal{D}$. Finally, we explore the relationship between the normal and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ in the context of a specific weighted directed graph, and we provide an example that highlights the variability of the depth of the normal powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ along with the variation of its vertex set.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved high accuracy in various image classification tasks and have become a fundamental component in many deep learning systems that rely on robust vision. While CNNs have shown great potential in areas like object detection, autonomous driving, and robotics, their susceptibility to faults in hardware makes them unreliable for critical applications. Previous studies have explored fault tolerance in CNNs with limited precision, but these methods primarily focus on numerical analysis without addressing the underlying mathematical representation of CNNs. In contrast, this work examines the efficacy of activation interval supervision in CNNs, exploring how it affects performance and robustness in the presence of hardware errors. Our findings show that, across four different CNN architectures and three image classification datasets, activation interval supervision yields comparable accuracy to standard training with a narrower activation interval range. Furthermore, we establish that activation interval supervision provides a security guarantee $\left(\frac{|x_i - \tilde{x}_i|}{\Delta x_i}\leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ in expectation, where $x_i$ and $\tilde{x}_i$ represent the original and corrupted values of the $i$th neuron, and $\Delta x_i$ denotes the width of the activation interval. This security guarantee holds without overestimation and is validated through simulations. In practice, this approach leads to a more compact representation with minimal overhead, specifically an average reduction of 2.5\% in the number of neurons and 4.3\% in the number of connections across all experiments. This work demonstrates that activation interval supervision offers a tangible improvement in performance and efficiency with a corresponding enhancement in robustness in the presence of hardware errors. In particular, we propose a simple yet efficient method called ReLU Cut, which involves determining the optimal width of the activation interval for each individual neuron by analyzing the distribution of its input weights. In cases where access to weight information is limited, we recommend a more straightforward approach called Uniform Cut, which involves determining a fixed width for all neurons based on the distribution of the input data. In both scenarios, we provide theoretical and simulation-based validation of the proposed approaches. Our research examined the production of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at a 5.44 TeV nucleon-nucleon energy. We compared our findings with proton-proton data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon energy and lead-lead data at a 2.76 TeV nucleon-nucleon energy. Our results showed a significant increase in particle production in Xe-Xe collisions compared to proton-proton data, and a smaller difference when compared to lead-lead data. We also observed a similar transverse momentum distribution slope (dN/dy) in Xe-Xe and lead-lead collisions. Furthermore, we found that the average number of phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions was 106 times greater than in proton-proton collisions, and that the ratio of phi meson production to pion production remained relatively constant across different energy levels. Additionally, we found that the ratio of phi meson production to pion production in central Xe-Xe collisions was 1.7 times greater than in central lead-lead collisions. Our research laid the groundwork for further study of mid-rapidity particle production in Xe-Xe collisions.

This research uses a mathematical model to simulate the large-scale protests in Chile during October 2019. This epidemiological-based model, inspired by viral transmission dynamics, accounts for participants' physical and geographical characteristics by treating roads as high-risk zones and public transportation as a critical transmission channel. A key feature of the model is the inclusion of a non-local transmission term, reflecting the spread of information and protests within the population. By integrating this aspect, the model demonstrates how protests can become widespread and sustained through the dissemination of information about events happening in distant locations. Our numerical solutions match real-world data on protest participation numbers and reveal the significance of non-local effects, transportation network influence, and a temporary external stimulus in explaining the protests' development. This model provides a framework for studying similar large-scale social phenomena driven by information and external influences. It also highlights the potential risks of unrest in large, complex societies with intricate transportation networks and far-reaching communication networks. Our findings are consistent with historical precedents, such as the 1964 Harlem riots in New York City and the 1992 Los Angeles riots. Our research offers a starting point for exploring other large-scale social phenomena, including the spread of infectious disease, as well as the dynamics of population migration and urban development. It also suggests that transportation network optimization may help mitigate and terminate large-scale social unrest events. Our code is available online. A hybrid visual-inertial navigation system can provide both position and orientation information at rates independent of GPS, using only camera and accelerometer sensor data. This method has significant potential for applications in augmented reality, drones, and autonomous vehicles. Previous studies using this technology have been limited to low-speed movements with significant access to visual data. To address this limitation, this research introduces a new hybrid VIO framework called EMA-VIO that utilizes external memory attention for efficient navigation in low-light environments. The proposed model leverages a compact state representation and combines visual and inertial features using external memory attention, resulting in improved accuracy under challenging lighting conditions. The evaluation of EMA-VIO shows that it achieves superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods in both outdoor and indoor settings with limited and intense lighting, respectively. The proposed method's efficiency is also demonstrated through a reduced computation cost. The code for EMA-VIO has been made publicly available on GitHub. The model's ability to operate at 30Hz using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU makes it suitable for real-time applications. The evaluation of a more complex model shows that EMA-VIO can achieve an accuracy of 0.8m in 3D position and 2.5° in orientation with just 10 frames of visual data. The model can be improved further by incorporating additional visual data, which would likely result in an even higher accuracy of 0.4m in 3D position and 1.5° in orientation. The proposed research provides a starting point for the development of visual-inertial navigation systems for various augmented reality applications. This study addresses the numerical solution to a data completion problem in electrodynamics, where the aim is to recover missing information of a physical source given incomplete measurement data, specifically for the scenario where the source or the observation point is not fully accessible due to physical obstacles. This problem is formulated as an inverse problem for a partial differential equation (PDE), specifically the non-stationary Maxwell equations, with the goal of determining a source term in the equations given incomplete boundary measurements. Since the forward Maxwell equations are ill-posed, typically an regularized approach is employed to solve the inverse problem. However, it results in a new, more complex PDE to solve, which requires a high level of precision to be solved numerically. A method based on a quasi-reversibility technique is proposed to simplify this task, and the effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical experiments using finite elements. The results show that this approach can recover a source with an accuracy of over 90% even when the data is significantly incomplete, and that the method is robust to various mesh sizes and time step lengths. The proposed approach can be adapted for static cases, and the code developed is available online. The study also highlights potential applications of this method in real-world scenarios, such as recovering missing data in incomplete measurements of electromagnetic fields in 3D, and imaging targets in radar and sonar. The method proposed has a significant advantage over alternative approaches like the Tikhonov method and the Landweber method, as it can recover missing data in a shorter time and with a lower level of noise. In the context of expanding knowledge bases through federated learning, a method called Federated Selective Integration for Knowledge Fusion has been developed. This approach enables the creation of new, high-quality knowledge base entries by selectively combining entries from participating institutions, without requiring the exchange of raw data. Federated Selective Integration addresses several challenges, including managing privacy and avoiding data duplication. It does this through a multi-stage process, starting with an initial comparison of entries, followed by a phase of data aggregation, and finally, a validation stage to ensure the accuracy of the combined entries. Experimental results using real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of Federated Selective Integration, revealing improvements of up to 20% in precision and 15% in recall when compared to alternative methods. The integration of terahertz frequency nanoscopy with planar microwave components, such as resonators found in microwave integrated circuits, holds significant promise for enhanced reliability, performance, and safety in various applications including filters, oscillators, and amplifiers. To achieve this, we have conducted a terahertz near-field nanoscopy analysis of a representative planar microwave resonator using a bow-tie antenna-equipped terahertz scanning microscope. The resulting high-resolution terahertz images provided a clear understanding of the local field distribution, dielectric material characteristics, and surface roughness of the resonator. The collected data also enabled us to accurately identify the frequency corresponding to a particular spatial location within the resonator. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the capability to remotely measure the dielectric constant of a material at a specific location using terahertz frequency nanoscopy. The success of this approach has implications for the quality control and design of planar microwave components. The terahertz near-field nanoscopy technique can be particularly useful for detecting defects, determining the frequency of operation, and assessing the performance of planar microwave resonators in the development and manufacturing stages. The methodology presented in this work can be applied to various types of planar microwave components, not just resonators. The code used for the simulations and analysis is publicly available on GitHub. The detection of a gravitational wave signal resulting from the merger of a neutron star and a black hole necessitates the analysis of large amounts of data. Due to the complexity of such data, machine learning algorithms are crucial in efficiently identifying potential signals. In this research, we utilize a 4-parameter model to describe binary mergers involving a neutron star and a black hole. We employ a neural network to classify 16 different combinations of neutron star-black hole parameters, with results showing improved performance over traditional methods. For instance, our neural network achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.36 for B-polarization modes, surpassing the 10.98 achieved with a 4-parameter model. Moreover, the neural network effectively distinguishes real data from simulated waveforms, with a 99.99% accuracy rate. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal neural network architecture and find that a 4-layer network with 64 nodes in each layer yields the best performance. Lastly, the neural network is trained to classify real data from simulated waveforms with a 99.99% accuracy rate, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications. This research is an initial step towards developing a more advanced neural network capable of analyzing more complex data, such as post-merger waveforms from neutron star and black hole collisions. This could potentially enable the detection of these collisions through the analysis of gravitational wave signals. This research develops a theory of integration over locally convex terrains in n-dimensional space, extending the fundamental Stokes theorem to this context. Building on this generalization, we establish a connection with the theory of integration over polytopes in $\mathbb{R}^n$, defining the integral of a differential form over a polytope as the sum of its integrals over the n-dimensional faces that make up the polytope's boundary. This relationship also enables us to generalize the concept of oriented polytopes to locally convex terrains, using the development of an appropriate terrain-integral transformation. By examining the preimage of a locally convex terrain under a differentiable map, we can further extend the theory to the context of oriented terrains and their associated integrals. This leads to the discovery that the integral of a differential form over the preimage of a locally convex terrain under a differentiable map can be expressed as the sum of the integrals of the form's pullback over the preimage of the terrain's n-dimensional faces, orientated according to their normal vectors. This result extends the Stokes theorem to locally convex terrains, demonstrating that the theorem is a generic property of the integral of a differential form over the preimage of a locally convex terrain under a differential map. This property can be seen as a manifestation of the topological invariant associated with the n-dimensional sphere, S^n. This interpretation is supported by the fact that changing the definition of the terrain-integral transformation by a factor of (1 - ε)^(n-1) will result in a change to the property, indicating that it is a property of the terrain-integral transformation in the space (1, ∞) rather than (1). This finding is further reinforced by examining the specific case of the map from the real line to the plane, y = f(x), which can be seen as a projection of the graph of the function onto the x-axis. This projection will yield a locally convex terrain if the function has a local maximum, and a convex polygon if the function has a saddle point. The integral of a differential form over the preimage of this terrain under the map can be calculated directly, and this calculation provides an alternative proof of the extension of the Stokes theorem to locally convex terrains. A common issue in sonar-based navigation arises from the varying quality of data, depending on whether it's obtained from a laser or a camera, due to different sensing ranges of these sensors. This disparity leads to navigation path inconsistencies, causing difficulties in creating a unified map. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method for immediately fusing sonar data, bypassing traditional registration and mapping steps. This approach, which employs a parametric model to describe the sonar scan, allows for direct insertion of sonar readings into the map without prior registration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in a simulation environment and on actual data from a Navigators X1 sonar, achieving a low error rate of 2.5%. This fusion technique can be utilized with a wide range of sonar sensors and provides a flexible framework for map construction, even with noisy data. Furthermore, this approach simplifies the integration of sonar data into existing navigation systems, offering a cost-efficient solution for many real-world applications. Experimental data and simulation codes are available online. This sonar fusion method has been applied in a real-world navigation scenario, detailed in a companion paper.

This algebraic form then serves as the basis for an iterative deconvolution procedure. The authors suggest that this framework provides a more robust method for selecting the number of components than standard information criteria. To break the "tower of glass" limiting further discovery at the Large Hadron Collider, it is essential to explore new approaches that can detect rare, high-energy events. A novel method, the "Elastic Potential" project, aims to achieve this by utilizing a specialized, highly sensitive neutrino rejection tool. This tool leverages a unique signature resulting from forward protons in elastic production of top quarks and their antiparticles, allowing for the identification of very rare processes that have been obscured by background noise. A proposed detector for the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, the Roman Puck detector, would be specifically designed to reject neutrinos and detect forward-scattered protons, enabling the detection of an annual rate of 0.1-1.0 Abas^2 of top-quark pairs through elastic production. This rate is significantly higher than predicted by existing simulations and highlights the "Elastic Potential" of this approach for uncovering rare processes at the Large Hadron Collider. The Roman Puck detector could be integrated into the ATLAS experiment during an upcoming upgrade, offering a flexible and cost-effective means of enhancing the LHC's discovery capabilities. The underlying technology for the Roman Puck detector, which utilizes a specialized, high-precision Roman pot detector design, could also be applied to future colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider. The "Elastic Potential" project offers a flexible framework for uncovering rare processes at the Large Hadron Collider, with the added benefit of enhancing our understanding of hadron-hadron interactions in the far-forward region. Given a finite non-abelian group G and a subgroup H of G, we define the algebraic diameter of H in G as the minimum number of conjugations required to transform H into a conjugate of H through elements of G. This measure is used to investigate the structural properties of groups and identify those with a specific diameter threshold (d ≥ 3). When d ≥ 3, we show that G has a specific composition structure and include examples of large groups with diameter d. Previously unknown results on the size of groups with a diameter of 3 or 4 are obtained. Specifically, we find that the number of elements in a group with a diameter of 3 is less than 3 times the number of elements in a symmetric group of the same degree, whereas the number of elements in a group with a diameter of 4 is less than 5 times the number of elements in a symmetric group of the same degree. Additionally, we provide lower and upper bounds for the number of elements in a group with a diameter of 3 or 4. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the diameter of a group and the simplicity of its permutation characters, and show that groups with a diameter of 3 or 4 have only two permutation characters, in addition to the trivial and regular characters. This implies that the number of irreducible character degrees in such groups is less than the number of elements in a symmetric group of the same degree, and that the number of irreducible character degrees in a group with a diameter of 3 is less than 3 times the number of elements in a symmetric group of the same degree. Finally, we provide an example of a simple group with a diameter of 4, and show that the number of elements in a simple group with a diameter of 3 or 4 is greater than the number of elements in a Berman-Suzuki group of the same degree.

This generalization enables us to apply framework constructions to a broader class of geometric situations, expanding the scope of the original concept. We have also explored the relationship between geometric frameworks and symplectic geometry within the context of symplectic and Poisson stacks, revealing that certain types of geometric frameworks are equivalent to specific collections of polytopes defined by local equations. These results provide a foundation for further investigations into the interplay between geometric frameworks, algebraic geometry, and combinatorial geometry. We have also developed a method for reconstructing Lie groupoids from geometric frameworks, which has implications for the study of rational curves and surface singularities. A statistical study of 106 infrared dark cores from the Dragon Shakhovsky infrared dark nebula reveals a distinct correlation between the cores' mass distribution and their surrounding external pressures. By examining this relationship under different mass regimes, we found that more massive cores tend to reside in areas with higher external pressures, suggesting a self-regulation mechanism that limits their growth. This self-regulation allows lower-mass cores to develop protostellar or prestellar mass spectra, whereas more massive cores may develop more massive spectra, potentially leading to the formation of high-mass stars. This hypothesis is supported by the detection of young stellar objects within the cores, with more massive cores exhibiting broader mass spectra that include higher mass ranges, and even evidence of massive protostars, a finding confirmed by additional submillimeter and mid-infrared observations. This self-regulation mechanism may be a key factor in the formation of high-mass stars and protostars, offering insights into how external pressures can influence the development of cores and ultimately the mass distributions of their contained stars. This study highlights the importance of studying the external pressures on cores and their surrounding environments in the formation of high-mass stars and protostars. This research also suggests that the formation of high-mass stars may be more likely in areas with denser molecular complexes like the Dragon Shakhovsky nebula, providing a new perspective on the formation conditions for high-mass stars. This study utilized data from the Dragon Shakhovsky infrared dark nebula observed by the 1.6 m telescope at the SAO RAS, along with additional data from the Herschel Space Observatory and the Spitzer Space Telescope. A key aspect of solving Poisson's equation for Hele-Shaw flow on the sphere is the computation of second moments of steady, random surface profiles under constant pressure. This calculation requires the solution to a specific second-order recurrence related to the sphere's geodesic triangulation. In this work, we derive an equivalent one-step recurrence for this purpose, specifically using a geodesic tetrahedral mesh. This approach allows for efficient numerical solutions, even with large resolutions. For the full sphere, we obtain an analytical one-step recurrence expression. Additionally, we investigate how different recurrence formulations behave in relation to resolution and computational time. This research also introduces an efficient algorithm for solving the Dirichlet problem for random fields on the sphere using recurrences, particularly useful for Hele-Shaw flow simulations. This algorithm employs a combination of recurrence solutions and polynomial interpolation, offering precise results for specified values and statistical averages. This research was motivated by the challenge of directly numerically solving the NSE-BLE equations for Hele-Shaw flow on the sphere, an approach that was found to be computationally expensive. An alternative method was developed, involving the use of recurrences to solve the Poisson equation for random surface profiles, and this approach was found to be more efficient. This research also explored different sphere triangulations and their impact on simulations, and identified a tetrahedral mesh as the most suitable option. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface characteristics, and studying this interaction can provide valuable insights into the behavior of various materials, from lotus leaves to liquid foams. Through a series of experiments involving the movement of a rigid plate through liquid foams on both smooth and textured surfaces, we have demonstrated a substantial increase in friction when using a textured surface, which is directly related to the displacement of air bubbles. This connection is further supported by calculations based on the distribution of stress within the foam. Additionally, we have observed that in situations where the air bubbles are more rigid, the enhancement in friction is more pronounced. This research highlights the importance of considering the texture's interaction with the internal structure of the liquid and its effects on the resulting friction. It also suggests that the texture-induced increase in friction is a general phenomenon affecting non-Newtonian liquids, which can be described by a dimensionless parameter that reflects the interplay between the texture's depth, the size of the air bubbles, and their rigidity. This finding has implications for understanding the behavior of liquids in various natural and engineered settings, including the flow of mud, the movement of sediment, and the performance of textured surfaces in medical devices. It also highlights the potential for designing surfaces with specific properties to manipulate the flow of complex liquids. A novel approach for identifying and removing outlier skin carcinoma samples using deep learning and entropy has been proposed. The method employs a combination of U-Net and a k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm to categorize skin carcinoma types and detect anomalous samples. Initially, a trained U-Net network is used to classify 21 types of skin carcinomas, and then the kNN algorithm determines the anomalous class assignments based on the Euclidean distance between the feature vectors. Outlier skin carcinoma samples are identified as those with more than five anomalous class assignments. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in detecting outlier skin carcinoma samples when compared to existing approaches using the Skin Lesion Analysis Towards Improved Diagnostics (SLICD) dataset. Specifically, our method shows a 10% improvement in accuracy, 12% in AUC-ROC, 15% in AUC-PR, and 20% in F1-score when evaluated on the validation set. Furthermore, when evaluated on the test set, our method exhibits a 5% improvement in accuracy, 8% in AUC-ROC, 10% in AUC-PR, and 15% in F1-score. The proposed method's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to leverage the inherent structure of data and minimize the impact of outlier samples on the model's performance. The proposed approach can be applied to various anomaly detection tasks beyond skin carcinoma analysis. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/krishnaiyer/Skin-Carcinoma-Anomaly-Detection. The dataset used in this research consists of 12,000 images, with 9,000 images used for training, 1,500 images used for validation, and 1,500 images used for testing. To enhance neural machine translation by addressing source-truncated issues, we propose a novel look-forward attention mechanism that enables the generation of target tokens to be informed by future source tokens. This innovative method allows for the incorporation of informative source contexts that might be cut off during the truncation process, leading to improved performance in restricted padding scenarios. We further explore the connection to existing attention mechanisms and discuss several look-forward mechanism variants. Experiments on four language pairs with different sentence length ratios reveal a performance boost of up to 3.5 BLEU points when source contexts are partially available, and our proposed mechanism also excels in unrestricted settings, demonstrating its versatility. In 1998, the Translating Framework was introduced to facilitate the integration of heterogeneous computing resources by translating high-level job descriptions into specific resource commands. This approach addressed the complexity and variability of distributed computing, allowing for more efficient and less error-prone job submissions. The Translating Framework influenced the development of grid computing, with many systems adopting similar approaches and utilizing the same standards, particularly the Job Description Language (JDL). As a result, the concept of translation became a fundamental aspect of grid computing, with standards like JDL becoming widely adopted. This paper explores the development of grid computing through the lens of the Translating Framework, examining the evolution of the concept and its impact on the field. This retrospective analysis highlights the key challenges faced by grid computing and the role of translation in addressing them, demonstrating how the Translating Framework's ideas have had a lasting impact on the field. This paper also discusses the current state of translation in grid computing, the remaining challenges, and potential future directions. This work is part of a larger effort to document the history of grid computing through the perspectives of its key contributors. Recent improvements in the understanding of $J/\psi$ mesons' decay into a photon, a neutral hadron, and nothing else have enhanced the accuracy of experiments searching for neutrino oscillations and dark photon signatures. Specifically, a more precise determination of $\BR(J/\psi\to \gamma\eta\to\gamma\gamma)$ is now possible. This development is particularly beneficial for the description of the $\eta$ meson within the chiral effective field theory, and it also offers a way to constrain the parameters of the $\eta$-dark photon effective vertex. As a result, this enhanced precision can be reflected in the estimates of neutrino and dark energy properties, leading to a prediction for $\BR(J/\psi\to \gamma\eta\eta)$ based on existing values for the masses of the $\eta$, $\eta'$, and dark photon. The interstellar medium is home to complex, high-latitude scintillation patterns caused by variations in the refractive index resulting from the movement of compact scintillometry observations in space. By analyzing the light curves of pulsar B1133+16, obtained through the LOFAR radio telescope over a 3-year period, researchers found a pattern of scintillation that remains relatively constant in both space and time. They identified a specific region of the interstellar medium, approximately 8 parsecs in diameter, that is characterized by a unique set of scintillation patterns. This finding is significant because it provides a localized three-dimensional map of the interstellar medium, including variations in plasma density and optical depth. Furthermore, the duration of the scintillation patterns suggests that this particular region of the interstellar medium is directly associated with a cloud of neutral gas, likely located within 1.5 parsecs from the Earth. This discovery is also notable because it allows for the calculation of the distance to this particular cloud of neutral gas, a value that is independently estimated to be 1.38 parsecs by analyzing the Doppler broadening of the pulsar's spectral lines. This particular cloud of neutral gas is part of a larger complex of neutral gas and plasma that is known as the Local Interstellar Dynamic Complex. This discovery highlights the value of scintillometry in creating detailed, three-dimensional maps of the interstellar medium, and it also underscores the importance of combining scintillometry with other observational techniques, such as spectroscopy, in understanding the structure and dynamics of the Local Interstellar Dynamic Complex. This research was conducted using data obtained from the LOFAR radio telescope over a 3-year period, and it demonstrates the telescope's ability to conduct long-term observations of the interstellar medium with compact scintillometry. Recently, generative models have achieved high-quality synthesis of speech and other sounds with specific characteristics. However, many of these models struggle with long-term dependencies and require large amounts of data for training and generation. To overcome these limitations, we present the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an autoregressive model based on the WaveNet architecture that uses pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks to capture both short and long-term patterns in audio. By alternating between small and large dilation periods, our model efficiently explores both the local and global structure of audio inputs. We demonstrate the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet's effectiveness on the LJSpeech dataset, achieving a mean opinion score of 4.25 for subjective quality assessment and 0.24 for subjective naturalness assessment. We also present an ablation study highlighting the benefits of our proposed design choices. The Quasi-Periodic WaveNet's simplicity and efficiency make it a competitive model for speech synthesis tasks. The code for the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is available at https://github.com/EsmeraldaG/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

This study focuses on an acoustic structure with an embedded elastic solid, where we aim to identify the elastic solid's properties based on measurements of the sound wave. Unlike previous approaches that determine the elastic solid's properties given its external boundary conditions, we will derive those boundary conditions from the measured sound data. By transforming the fundamental equations into a weak formulation within a computational framework, we use the Lasserre family of moments to approximate the solution and retrieve the elastic solid's properties. A numerical example illustrates the feasibility of this method. Additionally, we discuss a related issue involving the recovery of an elastic solid's properties from scattered acoustic waves, and offer a modified approach to tackle this related problem. A numerical example for this case shows the proposed method's effectiveness. A comparative study with a nonlinear least-squares solver using acoustic differential equations as a reference is also presented. A key advantage of this method is its ability to handle complex partial differential equations by treating the problem as a series of polynomial optimizations. This approach provides an alternative to traditional solvers based on numerical differentiation and matrix operations. This method can be applied to various inverse problems involving the recovery of elastic solid properties from measured data, including problems involving scattering, radiation, and other external influences. This study demonstrates the proposed method's effectiveness for a wide range of problems, and offers a framework for tackling other related problems. The rapid spread of COVID-19 necessitates the swift development of tools to aid in disease diagnosis and image-based analysis for its management. Deep learning techniques, particularly using pre-trained models on modified medical images, offer a promising approach to address this challenge. Here, we explore the potential of manipulating chest X-rays to enhance the effectiveness of classification networks in identifying different illnesses. In particular, we investigate several image processing techniques to add artificial lesions to normal chest X-rays and evaluate the performance of a trained classification model on these modified images. Our findings reveal that adding synthetic lesions to X-rays can significantly improve the model's accuracy in distinguishing healthy cases from those with lung lesions. Furthermore, we find that the most effective method of image modification is adding circular artificial lesions, which results in an improvement of 12.4% in the average classification score compared to using raw images. Our research provides a foundation for exploring the connection between image processing and classification models and highlights the potential of this approach for tasks such as predicting the location of lesions on chest X-rays.
